To study the impact of accidents or sudden loads on materials, it is necessary to examine their nonaffine elastic behavior outside the linear regime. However, determining experimental values for nonaffine parameters that occur during this process poses a significant challenge. A major issue arises from the fact that nonaffine disarrangement cannot change the material's macroscopic appearance, which makes direct measurement difficult. Nevertheless, if nonaffinity were present, fluctuations in density or pressure would also be expected to occur. Therefore, to investigate this, we subjected 3D printed blocks to shocks and studied the resulting deformation and fragmentation as well as local changes in density throughout the process. By applying the dynamical pore-fracture model to elasto-plastic materials subject to shocks, we can further confirm nonaffine disarrangement in the elastic phase through simulation. As a result, we were able to validate experimentally, for the first time, nonaffine disarrangement occurring at speeds around the material's shear wave speed and extending up to a significant fraction of the material's intrinsic nonlinear deformation range. This was also accompanied by evidence for disarrangement occurring in the material's core even when core density changes are not fully expected according to the model. Importantly, this experimental validation allowed for a more accurate calculation and confirmation for various nonaffine parameters that occur during sudden loading. Moreover, a notable observation was that nonaffine disarrangement led to significant shear deformation in previously thought fully incompressible materials, which in turn affected overall material pressure and density to a significant degree. Nonetheless, it did not give rise to significant changes in material appearance or overall deformation, which highlights an important role for quantitative imaging measurements in order to detect nonaffine behavior in experimental studies, especially in materials sciences where material fluids are commonly studied. Moreover, we were able to further refine our understanding of how pressure builds up inside solid materials when subjected to sudden external pressure, which may have significant implications for geophysical studies such as volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and comet impacts. Finally, by analyzing experimental results in terms of nonaffine parameter values, we were able to further confirm a theoretical prediction regarding a significant nonaffine parameter values that occur near failure, which may have significant implications for a wide variety of engineering and natural phenomena such as bridges, towers and asteroids.

This phenomenon existed between 120-180 MHz and seemed correlated with celestial objects experiencing high magnetic fields. A sub-set of these observations exhibited a correlation between low-frequency radio energy and extragalactic sources displaying significant polarization. Furthermore, the array detected varying levels of the radio sky's surface curvature, depending on both right ascension and frequency. This irregular pattern was likely caused by a combination of both magnetoionic phenomena caused by foreground sources and actual distant sources experiencing strong magnetic fields. A positive correlation was established between the low-frequency radio energy's surface curvature and the median polarization of radio sources, reaching as high as 20%. In numerous fields, probabilistic entropy serves as a fundamental measure of uncertainty, also appearing as a security metric in various cryptographic protocols. However, to offer genuine security assurances, the entropy source must be scrutinized in depth. This article assesses the integrity of basic sources, generated from classical bits, by examining their consistent and consistent-to-weak variations using multiple criteria, including concavity, strong subadditivity, and information-based inequalities. Consequently, specific references to practical entropy estimation methods will be reevaluated, alongside analyses of their potential vulnerabilities. Furthermore, this study proposes an alternative, consistent source family, also examined in terms of its causal characteristics. Ultimately, the article demonstrates that current source models are flawed and in need of a more nuanced, causal approach. It's hoped that this will contribute to the development of dependable security systems in the future. This investigation is part of a larger examination, detailed in the companion paper. In that work, a thorough investigation of stochastic consistency will be conducted, alongside an examination of causes and their role in information theory. We introduce a novel approach to integrate the NDT representation with deep learning techniques for efficient place recognition in point clouds. Our method leverages the computational efficiency of point cloud descriptors and the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks to effectively tackle the challenge of place recognition. Unlike previous descriptor-based methods, which often rely on memory-intensive data storage or complex ranking methods, our place recognition model utilizing NDT representation outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, including neural network-based methods, for both 3D loop closure and visual place recognition tasks. Our results demonstrate the superiority of the model, confirmed by both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. The implementation details can be found at the repository https://github.com/Keylt/3DPlaceRecNDT. Our research further investigates the impact of NDT parameters on representation efficacy and evaluates the robustness of NDT point clouds under varying noise levels. The findings reveal that NDT partition density has a substantial influence on representation accuracy. Additionally, our noise robustness analysis across four point cloud filters indicates that NDT is relatively insensitive to high noise levels compared to other techniques. The substantial computational savings of our model make it more feasible for implementation on embedded systems. Furthermore, our model's adaptability to scenarios with limited GPS and IMU data makes it more applicable to real-world conditions. The place recognition models discussed in this study are trained using the EuRoC and TIGA datasets as well as the ANTILOPE dataset, which was developed specifically for the ANTILOPE challenge. The models studied in this research exhibit a high degree of similarity, which implies that their weights can be transferred across various datasets captured from various sources, thereby reducing place recognition time. The results of our model demonstrate that a combination of sensor data, such as data from large-format sensors like the Reo! 60, can be effectively integrated to enhance place recognition performance. The analysis of functional network connectivity has become a critical tool for distinguishing individuals, detecting disease-related network patterns, and understanding cognitive functions. The key assumption in this research is that the underlying network patterns can be reliably estimated through single subject data analysis. However, the role of inter-site effects in this estimation process has yet to be fully evaluated. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis of inter-site effects on Estimation Bias (EB) and Variability (EV) in multi-site functional network connectivity analysis. Our findings suggest that inter-site effects have a significant impact on both EB and EV. Specifically, EB can reach up to 20-30% and variability up to 50-60% in particular scenarios. To enhance network estimation reliability, we develop a weighted average approach that combines individual network estimates from multiple sites. Our results indicate that this weighted average technique substantially reduces both bias and variability. Finally, we demonstrate that by combining EB and EV metrics with p-values and network test statistics, we can enhance the reliability of accuracy rates in multi-site data analysis. The techniques and findings presented can be applied across various neuroimaging domains including resting-state fMRI, rs-fMRI, and diffusion tensor imaging. This research investigates the effectiveness of position-based data augmentation methods to improve the accuracy of code-mixed language models. Three position-based averaging techniques are examined which involve combining consecutive text segments with varying lengths to generate new sentences. The study finds that applying these techniques yields improved language models, both with and without cross-regularization, and outperforms positionally blind data augmentation methods on Wikipedia tasks in multiple code-mixing scenarios. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate the benefits of incorporating positionally informed data augmentation in cross-regularization-based models. The findings also suggest that position-based data augmentation can be efficiently applied to parallel corpora, like the newly developed Hindi-English Wikipedia dataset. The study provides insights that can inform the design of more efficient code-mixed language modeling systems. The research is applicable across various code-mixing languages and can be readily applied to real-world tasks. The proposed positional encoding-based data augmentation method may also offer significant improvements in applications such as named entity recognition, machine translation, sentiment analysis, information extraction, and others. Our research in simulated hydride clusters using quantum chemical methods indicates that at high pressures, both reactions contribute equally, resulting in an expected isotope effect. At lower pressures, however, the three-body reaction dominates, contributing a relatively large $\eta$ value. These findings support recent experimental results that indicated a significant $\eta$ value at 100 GPa, but a much smaller value at lower pressures. In complex environments with restricted access to spatial constraints through sensors, navigating via motion planning becomes more challenging. To tackle this issue, researchers have introduced a novel approach that generates high-resolution spatial constraints using coarser-grained maps and multiple sensors. The proposed method significantly boosts motion planning efficiency and performance, yielding a notable 16x and 23x improvement in speed and accuracy respectively. Moreover, when implemented on a real-world robotic setup, this approach results in a 45% decrease in the number of collisions and an 84% increase in successful landings. We will examine this approach in further detail. 

To start, the spatial constraints are derived from a 3D point cloud by first breaking it down into horizontal layers, which are then segmented into spatial areas based on their coherence levels. The sensor data for these areas is analyzed to establish the coherence levels, thereby creating a grid-based representation of spatial constraints. The width of this grid is adjustable and influences the spatial constraints' resolution.

The spatial constraints' nature can be varied by defining a coherence pipeline, which processes the point cloud data. The pipeline comprises various modules that convert 3D point cloud data into distinct spatial constraints such as occupancy information (e.g., ground plane, canonical surface), floor plans, and even semantic data. The spatial constraints are represented as occupancy maps with an adjustable level of granularity.

Once the spatial constraints are derived, they are used to create a grid-based map that is fed into a pathfinder. The pathfinder generates a motion plan based on the spatial constraints, which in turn, facilitates the creation of a detailed 3D path that is validated using spatial constraints to ensure that it remains within specified boundaries.

The method significantly improves motion planning in cluttered environments, but it is primarily tailored for indoor environments, which might not be suitable for complex outdoor settings. The proposed approach, although effective, has its limitations in applicability to complex outdoor environments. Further research is needed to extend its feasibility to such scenarios. We analyze two distinct problems: a standard, full-bandwidth identification issue and a more complex, dimension-reduced one, involving the combination of power control and beamforming. We derive a multiple-block LS estimator for the first problem, showing it converges at the same rate as the optimal iterative LASSO method but takes significantly fewer iterations. For the second problem, we apply group LASSO approaches, also achieving faster convergence than the iterative LASSO baseline. Moreover, group LASSO methods prove particularly effective in reducing interference and increasing the sum-rate of MIMO systems with multiple users, outperforming traditional iterative LASSO methods. Additionally, we propose a novel LASSO-based algorithm for the downlink domain, addressing issues related to channel covariance uncertainty, which takes less computational time than iterative LASSO. We investigate the tropicalization of finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, leading to the concept of pull-back of rational function semifields. Contrary to the case of non-tropical settings, the fiber of the rational function semifield over a point may be a more complex object - a semifield. We establish that if the characteristic of the field we're working in is zero, then the rational function semifield can be represented as the intersection of a specific type of linear system's pull-backs. Based on this, we find a new description for the tropicalization of finite harmonic mappings, involving the geometric properties of tropical divisors. Additionally, we expand our findings to develop an algorithm that allows us to compute the tropicalization of finite harmonic mappings, building on Bala&Gonzalez-Stein's previous work. The algorithm also enables us to verify that certain types of tropical divisors are associated with rational function semifields, rather than simply being generic tropical divisors. Furthermore, we define and prove a tropical version of the Riemann-Roch theorem for curves, providing a connection between tropical geometric properties and algebraic characteristics of curve functions. The study also addresses related problems concerning tropical modular forms on tropical curves, resulting in the description of a specific type of tropical modular form - the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya wavefront multifunction. We establish that any multifunction arising from wavefronts of holomorphic functions is a tropical modular form if it has a specific vanishing condition on a curve called the 'Appell hyperurface'. In a last section, we explore the application of multivariate tropical modular forms to solve the multivariate tropical Kapranov conjecture, concerning the properties of holomorphic functions on curves. We demonstrate that any multifunction arising from wavefronts of multivariate holomorphic functions meets the requirements for a multivariate tropical modular form, proving the Kapranov conjecture. Similar to the case of univariate functions, we identify the geometric properties of tropical divisors as the key to understanding the algebraic characteristics of multivariate curve functions. The findings also imply that any multivariate tropical modular form is associated with a specific type of linear system - complete linear systems. By pulling back these forms to their pull-backs, we create new multivariate tropical forms, resulting in yet another geometric property of tropical divisors. This research focuses on finding a specific condition that guarantees the existence of a unique, exponentially converging quasi-stationary $\pi$-distribution for a Markov process. We consider various scenarios where assumptions about the Markov process's properties vary. In one scenario, assuming the Markov process is irreducible on its closed complement, we derive a criterion using a potential theory concept. In another scenario, assuming the Markov process is a time-homogeneous Markov chain, we derive a criterion based on its reciprocal functions. We discuss connections between these criteria and criteria developed by Borovkov and Darling-Newman for absorbing boundary conditions and provide examples to demonstrate the applicability of these findings. We also explore scenarios where a Markov process has multiple distinct quasi-stationary $\pi$-distributions that differ in number and specific values. In one such example, a Markov process that is not irreducible on its closed complement, we show that even though its equilibrium distribution is a singular point measure with a single point, it is surrounded by an infinity of distinct quasi-stationary measures. By extracting word embeddings from these visual sources, rare words in text can be represented more effectively, primarily by distinguishing similar sounding words. The methodology consists of a visual-based word clustering method that identifies words sharing similar visual characteristics, such as "door" and "window," and incorporates this semantic understanding into language models through type-level context. To achieve this, a novel attention mechanism is introduced, allowing the model to prioritize type-level information over style-level context, which is also captured through a transformer-based architecture. The experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in boosting rare word recognition and overall sentence accuracy. Furthermore, the model's capability to absorb rare word knowledge from visual sources highlights its potential as a standalone rare word identification tool. The source code and dataset will be publicly accessible.

Additionally, we propose a set of best practices to enhance the privacy of collaborative models in real-world applications. Our research contributes to the ongoing efforts to protect personal data in machine learning and signals the need for further research in statistical inference, particularly in the context of privacy, mathematics, and learning paradigms such as vertical federated and horizontal federated learning. Graph Neural Networks have achieved remarkable success in semi-supervised node classification. The semi-supervised setting involves training models on a small set of labeled nodes and predicting classifications for a larger, unlabeled set. Recently, pseudo-labeling has emerged as a prominent approach for effectively utilizing unlabeled data. Standard pseudo-labeling methods typically prioritize high-confidence predictions, often disregarding uncertain labels, which can hinder GNN performance in classification. To counter this, we propose an improved pseudo-labeling strategy called PGL, which aims to assign more confident labels to challenging, uncertain nodes by leveraging the collective support of multiple labeled nodes. PGL combines a traditional score function with a metric derived from the label's neighborhood to calculate the confidence of a predicted label. This paper employs a control approach grounded in the properties of its component parts to investigate the behavior of a robot navigating along a straight wall, assuming it is moving away from the wall. The wall-following robot is equipped with a rear-facing distance sensor and its trajectory is influenced by the field of view provided by this sensor. Two distinct control approaches are examined: a model-based control, which utilizes a simplified mathematical representation of the robot, and a data-driven control, which relies on the analysis of the sensor data to calculate the steering angle. The open-loop and closed-loop trajectories resulting from these controls are compared, particularly with respect to the field of view and how the robot interacts with its surroundings. The findings suggest that the model-based control offers greater precision and versatility, but it is limited to specific environmental conditions, whereas the data-driven control is more adaptive and efficient, but it does not benefit from the insights provided by the robot's mathematical representation. Furthermore, the trajectory analysis reveals that the robot exhibits curved paths when equipped with a wide-angle sensor, which significantly deviates from the straight-and-forward navigation trajectory observed in sensors with narrow fields of view. The approach also addresses the issue of the robot straying from its course by identifying the threshold beyond which the sensor's field of view significantly impacts the robot's trajectory, causing it to veer off path. The corresponding trajectories resulting from the open-loop and closed-loop controls are analyzed using both model-based and data-driven control strategies. The findings suggest that the robot's trajectory is accurately reproduced in all four approaches, which supports the validity of the control approaches and the open-loop and closed-loop trajectories calculated using the model-based and data-driven control strategies. The comparison also highlights the differences in the control parameters and their environmental dependence, which must be taken into account when designing a straight-and-forward navigation algorithm for a wall-following robot equipped with a wide-angle sensor. The approach offers greater precision, adaptability, and efficiency in the open-loop and closed-loop controls, which can be applied to a variety of robots equipped with wide-angle sensors to promote safer and more autonomous navigation. The corresponding source codes for the model-based and data-driven control strategies are available for public access and can be used by researchers and practitioners to tackle related control and robotics challenges. The source codes can be accessed through the repository at https://github.com/antugdj/robot-control-walls-following. The study's findings highlight the need for consistent and precise modeling to produce straight-and-forward wall-following navigation trajectories, particularly for robots equipped with wide-angle sensors.

As a rapidly expanding field, radiomics analysis is expected to play a critical role in personalized cancer diagnosis and treatment in the future. However, the complexity of image analysis on a large scale poses significant challenges, primarily due to the computational intensity of quantitative techniques and the limited spatial resolution of commonly used clinical imaging methods. To overcome these obstacles, a high-performance computing platform-based solution is proposed, integrating advanced multi-threading and accelerated technologies such as OpenCV, Caffe, and GPU cups to significantly enhance analysis efficiency. By leveraging these state-of-the-art tools, the proposed platform achieves high-throughput quantitative radiomics analysis capabilities, including automatic image processing, feature extraction, and data optimization at speeds of up to 10-100 times faster than previous systems, all within a framework of customizable code. To test the performance of the platform, a comprehensive set of 255,845 images from 1021 patients were analyzed, producing 3,651,980 feature values that were further processed into 96,517 texture images and 162,715 volume images based on specified rules. These results revealed that the platform is capable of supporting multiple simultaneous analyses, while offering precise statistical summaries, parameter distributions, and correlation analysis. To our knowledge, this research represents the first successful application of a high-performance platform to large-scale radiomics analysis, achieving a speed of 10 seconds per image on an ordinary graphics card. We believe that this breakthrough has significant implications for radiomics data analysis in large-scale studies, potentially reducing analysis time from hours or days to seconds or minutes. The proposed platform is entirely open-source, providing a foundation for further innovation and research in this field. The complete source code is available for download at https://github.com/NeuropathLAP/rp-HPC. Input data and results can be accessed at https://napkiuhk.gitbook.io/rp-hpc/. While machine learning success relies heavily on data preparation, there is a lack of tools to evaluate and refine these processes. Currently, there is no standardized method to assess the effectiveness of data pre-processing pipelines, or to update them based on new information. This paper introduces a new approach to analyze pre-processing pipelines using statistical analysis and visualization tools, and to identify areas for improvement by detecting inconsistencies in data distribution across various samples. This innovative method can also track changes to pre-processing pipelines, and align data preparation with shifting data characteristics. Furthermore, the technique can be extended to incorporate real-time feedback from human reviewers, and is demonstrated by an in-depth examination of a specific use case involving image classification for renewable energy applications. The results show that by continuously refining the pre-processing pipeline, there are significant improvements in classification accuracy and coverage rates, and that the technique can be used to balance the trade-off between accuracy and coverage. The paper also discusses potential extensions to further enhance the method. Additionally, the system introduced in this paper has the following key benefits: (i) it allows for automatic analysis and improvement of pre-processing pipelines, (ii) it provides real-time feedback on sample-specific discrepancies, (iii) it allows for parallel analysis of numerous datasets, (iv) it can be combined with human feedback mechanisms, and (v) it can be used as an educational tool to teach data pre-processing and machine learning. The technique and implementation are openly available at https://github.com/koop-olsen/pipevision. Lastly, the study discusses challenges and limitations of the technique, including potential avenues for further improvement. We develop a novel framework combining structural learning and inference to comprehend the intricate dynamics of student course enrollment. By assuming course prerequisites form a tree, we train a Gaussian model to predict which courses students take, given their prior backgrounds and the current academic structure. Our approach simultaneously estimates factors influencing enrollment patterns, such as interest and tree compliance, at both individual and course levels. We achieve this using a two-step Bayesian procedure involving Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms. We also demonstrate how our framework can be used for various purposes like generating simulated enrollment data, recommending course changes, and providing personalized advice on course offerings. We evaluate the performance and accuracy of our model using simulated and actual data from Stanford University. Our results demonstrate that the model effectively identifies key factors underlying enrollment decisions and generates realistic simulated data. Furthermore, the recommendations generated by our model are both accurate and relevant, aligning with existing enrollment patterns while taking into account individual differences. Based on our analysis, we suggest the model's confidence level when providing recommendations. The proposed framework can potentially be applied to other large complex networks that involve variable arities of edges, such as student professor or computer system network interactions. We anticipate that our approach will be beneficial in understanding and visualizing such networks. The implementation details and source code of our model can be found at this website: <https://github.com/shalinvara/enrollmentframework>. A mathematical model for a simplified vehicle trajectory plan is developed as a two-player game. This game's solution, in turn, inspires an open-closed loop control strategy, which can be interpreted through Pontryagin's principle. As the outer loop, the long-term outcome determines an equilibrium state, known as Nash equilibrium, while the inner loop follows the path to reach that equilibrium, understood as a time-optimal control strategy along the equilibrium path. This approach is applied to a specific case at the German Digital Fleet Initiative's test site, where numerical calculations reveal a time-optimal trajectory to be approximately 2.7 seconds faster than the one obtained through linear control methods. Additionally, the model helps to identify constraints limiting the time-optimal trajectory, thereby allowing for the calculation of a second-best Nash equilibrium. This phenomenon indicates that in certain scenarios, a player may choose an equilibrium other than the optimal one, even if they could have achieved a faster time, due to these constraints. Consequently, this finding suggests that linear control strategies may miss the mark by not accounting for these constraints, thus resulting in an equilibrium that is not the optimal one, even in a straight-line test site. This outcome highlights the necessity of considering non-cooperative behavior in the design of platooning systems. Lastly, this method can be extended to a multi-player game, though the associated open-closed loop control strategy in this context remains an area for further investigation. This study contributes to the field of autonomous vehicle systems by providing an analytical framework, originally designed for the purpose of controlling platoons, which can also analyze Nash equilibria and time-optimal strategies in the existing traffic conditions, even when vehicles are not closely aligned. As traffic conditions continue to deteriorate due to congestion, this analysis identifies equilibria corresponding to the local maxima of an equilibrium's velocity, which, in turn, corresponds to the velocity at which the system's constraints are fully utilized, which in this case, is approximately 120 km/h. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a time-optimal control strategy fails to significantly improve this velocity, which hints at a potential failure of time-optimal strategies to improve traffic conditions, which will worsen further as vehicles approach higher speeds, such as 150 km/h, where a failure of time-optimal strategies to effectively reduce travel time is observed. To explore the limitations of contemporary AI and protect human credibility online, we have developed a framework for creating AI-generated human-like headlines and conducted an experiment where human evaluators scored these generated headlines alongside genuine ones on reliability. The results showed that AI-generated headlines consistently received higher credibility ratings than their human counterparts, often by a significant margin. Furthermore, the research revealed that state-of-the-art transformer models are surprisingly ineffective at distinguishing between human and computer-generated text, suggesting a need for further improvement in language representation. Building on successful applications in image manipulation detection, we have established a benchmark dataset called DEEP HUMAN and will make its training data and associated code publicly available in order to support research in this area. The dataset can be accessed at https://deephuman.github.io/. The training code can be found at https://github.com/ASTOASTO/DEPHUMAN-Challenge. Created with the aim of advancing research in this field, the DEPHUMAN-Challenge benchmark will serve as a platform for researchers to develop more accurate natural language processing systems that can effectively identify and counter AI-generated content. The incorporation of state-of-the-art language models into the training dataset has significantly enhanced their ability to accurately classify and generate human-like text. Notably, the trained GPT-2 model was observed to consistently produce better results than human-generated headlines in various evaluation metrics, including BLEU and SemEval scores. The successful application of the transformer model in this context highlights its limitations in the context of deepfake detection, where it has been repeatedly outperformed by its own predictions. The use of real-time calibration schemes in large-N arrays that have redundant antennas can be efficient in eliminating systematic errors that affect antenna gains. However, calculating the gains in real-time comes with a cost, particularly with the antenna gains becoming more unpredictable as the time needed for calibration increases. In scenarios where significant time is required for calculating the gains, using historical data to predict antenna gains may be a better approach despite the need for additional computation. By analyzing the effects of using calibration data on the variability of antenna gains, our research finds that gaining an extra minute of precision in gains requires about tenfold more computing power. Conversely, using historical data to predict gains leads to a manageable increase in computational demands but results in less precise gains. In fact, the precision in gains plateaus as the amount of data used to predict the gains increases. We also found that a balance must be found between the time spent calculating the gains and the variability of the gains, as extremely precise but time-consuming calculations may not be necessary given the resulting gains variability. Furthermore, the effectiveness of real-time calibration schemes in mid-frequency experiments is also discussed. Ultimately, the choice between using real-time calibration schemes or relying on historical data to predict the gains depends on a balance between the trade-offs of gain precision, variability, computational complexity, and the need for precise and reliable antenna gains. By analyzing these factors, our research provides guidance on the most appropriate approach for different arrays and use cases. In practice, the effectiveness of real-time calibration schemes in mid-frequency experiments that involve large-N arrays is also assessed, and the results reveal that these schemes can be efficient but only if the calculation process is not too time-consuming and the resulting gains show significant improvements relative to using historical data to predict the gains. In contrast, the use of real-time calibration schemes in smaller arrays that are used at higher frequencies may be a good approach because the resulting gains variability may not be a problem and the computational demands to calculate the gains may be manageable. In general, the effectiveness of real-time calibration schemes in smaller arrays that are used at higher frequencies shows more promising results, whereas their effectiveness in larger arrays that are used at lower frequencies may not be a good idea. The investment problem is addressed as an autoencoding-based ACGAN hybrid, merging the fields of portfolio optimization and deep learning. The hybrid minimizes portfolio volatility over time by learning the equilibrium between returns and risks from historical market data. As a result, the ACGAN's implicit loss function emulates the mean-variance portfolio and consequently reduces total risk through a Markowitz-like allocation. Furthermore, the risk management capability of ACGAN can also be attributed to its ability to learn and represent risk-free strategies, alongside effectively handling short positions. The outcomes demonstrate that the implicit Markowitz allocations derived from ACGAN, when contrasted with the explicit Markowitz allocations, based on the same historical data, exhibit lower total risk during subsequent periods. Therefore, the implicit allocations also effectively withstand various financial crises and market downturns. Nonetheless, ACGAN's implicit portfolio allocations exhibit a higher cross-sectional dispersion compared to the Markowitz allocations, likely resulting from an overfitting issue that may be resolved by dividing the investment dataset into a train-set and a test-set. Moreover, an implicit allocation's dependability also hinges on the quality of the pre-existing portfolio. This study thus introduces a retraining mechanism to guide ACGAN's learning towards an increased exploitation of the pre-existing portfolio's characteristics, thereby minimized allocation disparities. The implicit allocations derived from ACGAN also show a higher return-risk tradeoff compared to the Markowitz allocations, indicating ACGAN's ability to detect and capitalize on the equilibrium between returns and risks from historical market data. Finally, ACGAN's implicit portfolio allocations can also be attributed to an information-based trading style, specifically an autoencoding-style risk management approach. Bayesian neural networks are well-suited for classification in situations with limited or unbalanced data. They use a combination of Gaussian process and neural network priors to derive posterior distributions, which can be difficult to compute due to the non-closed form of the evidence and high computational complexity. We developed an approximation method based on variational inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to efficiently estimate the posterior distribution. Our method involves sampling a distribution by iterating over Markov chain steps before approximating the posterior uncertainty for classification. We validated the technique with experiments on widely-used datasets, such as MNIST, CIFAR10, and EMNIST, demonstrating accurate results and a significant reduction in computational time compared to exact calculations. Furthermore, we applied this method to classify Chlamydia psittaci protein families using balanced data and identified distinct subfamilies. The method yielded an accuracy of 75% with an F1-score of 75%, while an unbalanced random forest had an accuracy of 74% and an F1-score of 74%. These results demonstrate the potential for Bayesian neural networks to be used for classification of unbalanced data of microbial proteins, contributing to finding patterns in MCMV viruses, classifying microbe spectra, and identifying functional proteins. User-generated content on social media is abundant and constantly updated, offering a wealth of information on a wide array of topics. This content has significant marketing potential due to its potential reach of millions of users, but attempting to locate the desired content is increasingly difficult for users due to an overwhelming amount of data on visual platforms like Instagram. We have developed a prototype search engine that extracts posting trends from user profiles on Instagram, which dynamically adjusts based to provide the most relevant results. A user can access a user account and see relevant content in a simplified interface, bypassing the need to search individually. There are several key user and resource obstacles that must be overcome, including different user motivations and the resource constraints of both users and visual systems. These challenges are addressed through a single, user-centered interface that combines content and visual system functionality, relying on a cloud-based server for processing and storage. The system has been tested with 50 distinct themes and showcases how it can be achieved through a human-in-the-loop approach that addresses user and visual system constraints. The results of our evaluation indicate that 85% of users can locate the desired content within 2 seconds, with a mean rank of 6.22, and an accuracy rate of 90% in visual system classification. The system has shown remarkable performance, relying solely on user-generated metadata for image classification, outperforming current standards by more than 15%. The system also reports an accuracy rate of 93% in identifying content trends, with a mean rank of 7.14, surpassing current benchmarks by nearly 20%. The system's prototype demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in facilitating efficient content location on visual systems like Instagram. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm to calculate the Laplacian and Laplace-Beltrami tensors of weighted hypergraphs. Building on the tensor join concept, the proposed method simplifies the computation of higher-order tensor products, such as the Laplacian tensor, by partitioning the tensor elements into smaller pieces and combining them using joins. Diverging from its classical application in data analysis, the tensor join presents new methods for ordered structures. In this study, its application in ordered hypergraphs reveals new insights into their properties and the relationship between tensor join operations and spectral graph properties. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms demonstrate speed and memory efficiency by adapting to a hypergraph's structural characteristics, specifically the distribution of its hyperedges among different sizes. Moreover, the research explores the eigenvalues of the Laplacian tensor, establishes a hypergraph's expansion property, and develops a metric for approximating the volume of a weighted hypergraph. These findings have been incorporated into PyTera - a Python library for weighted hypergraphs - that provides utility functions, algorithms, and data structures for their study and offers a framework for its distribution through PyPI. PyTera can be extended through Python packages, facilitating its adoption by the research community. A comprehensive documentation is available online. The conventional approach analyzes such data using a variety of methods, such as mixed linear models, which treat the data as distinct observations, or use repeated measurements treated as repeated observations.  These methods can have drawbacks such as disregarding the correlated measurements that arise from repeated subjects, or ignoring the time-varying relationships within the data.  One potential solution is the use of constrained longitudinal data analysis with natural cubic splines.  This approach, though theoretically possible, is often too computationally intensive for practical use due to its computationally intensive nature.  Therefore, a shortcut is taken by approximating this analysis using a combination of low-order models applied to different sections of the data and then combining them, which can be efficiently analyzed via maximum likelihood.  In this paper, this approach is compared to other methods using data from the COPE study.  Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the traditional methods.  Specifically, the proposed method was found to consistently estimate certain parameters at a higher rate of accuracy than the other methods, though the rate of convergence varied depending on the parameter in question.  Moreover, the proposed method was found to consistently underestimate certain error parameters, but did converge at a higher rate for certain other error parameters.  In general, the proposed method was found to consistently outperform the traditional methods.  In addition, the proposed method was found to consistently outperform the other-time varying models, while converging at a higher rate than the model-free approach. A new approach to calculating chemical reaction pathways and their associated transition states has been developed, combining the space annealing algorithm for exploring different molecule shapes with a series of temporary intermediates. This approach, known as the temporary intermediate space annealing algorithm, was tested on several different systems including the reaction between ethylene and hydrogen, the dissociation of hydrogen molecules, and the reaction between methane and hydrogen. These simulations revealed that the pathway found through this new method was similar to one found through the exploration of different molecule shapes with no intermediates, but in a much shorter amount of time, resulting in calculations on over 1200 different shapes compared to only calculating 9 different shapes with no intermediates. Additionally, calculations indicated that the energy needed to break an ethylene hydrogen was already relatively low, around 64 kilojoules per mole, which is close to the energy needed to break a hydrogen molecule, which is around 109 kilojoules per mole, which suggests that ethylene reacts with hydrogen at the outer hydrogen through a loose transition state. In contrast, calculations suggested that ethylene reacts with temporary methane by moving one of its double bonds around the temporary methane through a loose transition state that is similar to one found through the exploration of different molecule shapes with no intermediates, which results in a reaction that looks very similar to one where an ethylene hydrogen is replaced with a methane hydrogen. Lastly, calculations suggested that hydrogen molecules dissociate in a step process where the molecule first breaks an impulse then the impulse breaks into three, which is results that differ from the findings of previous simulations, which found that the breaking of an impulse results in the breaking of another impulse around the same molecule, which results in a polyatomic radical. These results indicate that the space annealing algorithm combined with temporary intermediates is a highly efficient tool for calculating chemical reaction pathways and their associated transition states, which can result in new and novel reaction pathways being discovered. We establish novel Moser-type estimates for a class of nonlinear parabolic
Hessian equations, relate their $L^n$ ($n>1$) estimates to solutions of parabolic
Hessian equations, and derive several applications and improvements of existing
estimates, with an emphasis on the regularity of the solutions. The proof
relies on a parabolic nonlocal monotonicity estimate and a suitable truncation
technique. The regularity of the solutions is further refined using improved
$W^{k,2x}$ estimates for a range of $x$ values. Consequences of these estimates
include the optimal growth rate and regularity of the solutions to the
drift-diffusion-fokker-Planck equation and the optimal regularity of the solutions
to the parabolic complex Monge-Amp\`er equation. Moreover, our estimates provide a
new perspective on the regularity of the solutions to the parabolic complex
Monge-Amp\`er equation, an issue that has been extensively researched over two decades.

We demonstrate that any data type that can be expressed using Church encodings can also be expressed explicitly, and we establish a significant condition for achieving this typable expression. Our work builds on earlier research by Paul Levy and Ralf Hinze, expanding their results to include a more precise theoretical framework. We also explore connections between this study and relevant work in type theory, including uncurrying techniques and constructive data type recursion schemes. The uncovered proof significantly advances the understanding of this typable expression condition by replacing a previously complex infinite set of axioms with a single, straightforward one. This work also improves on and generalizes existing uncurrying techniques, and we identify a condition under which a type is expressive enough to include all exponentiation types. Additionally, we establish a connection between this study and the challenges of constructive data type recursion schemes as identified by Paul Levy. The uncovered proof also reveals that this typable expression condition is not solely a consequence of the presence of a type for natural numbers, and we demonstrate this by showing that removing this type does not affect the expressivity of the system while preserving its consistency. In this research, we explore the possibilities of expanding the theoretical boundaries of grant-free uplink access, specifically in terms of the number of users who can simultaneously transmit data to a single receiver via non-orthogonal sequences. To achieve this, we first identify the optimal sequence types that maximize the access spectrum efficiency, before investigating how to efficiently bundle sequences for multiple user allocations. Notably, non-orthogonal sequences can efficiently support a large number of users who can simultaneously transmit data to a single receiver, offering superior performance in terms of uplink delay and overall uplink performance when compared to more complex, grant-free methods such as deep sequencing-based approaches. Theoretical predictions are validated by real-world simulations, which reveal substantial gains - up to 80% - in uplink access performance when non-orthogonal sequences are used instead of the more complex, grant-free methods. Furthermore, our study also sheds light on key sequencing considerations, such as the importance of category-tail sequencing in ensuring balanced sequencing performance across various user groups. Overall, this paper provides crucial insights into sequencing best practices and lays the groundwork for sequential coding techniques that can be used across diverse channel conditions, from narrowband to wideband. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities and challenges associated with grant-free access research. This threshold can be set such that convergence is ensured at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/k^{2}\right)$. Grazing ecosystems, which are found in diverse locations worldwide, have been studied extensively due to their complex dynamics and widespread occurrence. Previous research, particularly that of Holling's diffusive movement hypothesis and subsequent studies, have explored how spatial factors influence these ecosystems' resilience to changes in aridity. Nevertheless, most of these studies have methodological limitations as they either analyze static or quasi-static systems, or rely on simplified statistical models, ignoring the ecosystems' spatial structure. We have developed a spatially extended, locally influenced model of grazing ecosystems that takes into account the spatial distribution of grazing parameters. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating spatial considerations significantly improves the ecosystems' resistance to harsher conditions, with a much smoother transition observed in the ecosystem's state between stability and chaos. Moreover, the ecosystem's resilience varies nonlinearly with the level of spatial consideration. Interestingly, our data suggest that ecosystem management strategies aimed at reducing instability may have opposite effects, as the ecosystem can actually be stabilized by limiting the spatial diffusion of grazing parameters. These results highlight the need to develop adaptive management practices, which take into account the ecosystems' spatial structure, to mitigate the effects of environmental changes. Holling's initial theory aimed to explain how diffusive movement affects ecosystem dynamics; our research offers a new perspective, that of a locally-influenced, spatially-scattered system, which provides insights into the long-range interactions within grazing ecosystems. Creating summaries from lengthy, unstructured texts with abstractive summarization comes with the challenge of inaccurately capturing the text's meaning due to a limited understanding of the context. A potential solution to address this issue is to represent a sequence of entities that were present during the summarization process. As a means of improving summary accuracy, we propose implementing a traditional planning framework known as the Why-Goal-Plan-Action (WGPA) framework. We develop our framework by identifying why a particular entity is important, setting relevant goals, plan the structure of the summary, and finally generate the summary actions. The results from experimentation on the Document Sum-mary (DocSum) dataset have indicated several key observations, including the significant improvement in extractive summarization performance when utilizing our entity chain-based approach, as well as the valuable contribution of human-annotated why-goal-plan (whyGP) pairs in enhancing WGPA output quality. Furthermore, we found that WGPA was capable of producing high-quality abstractive summaries by providing a whyGP pair that represented a portion of the summary content. Based on these outcomes, it appears that WGPA has the potential to be a valuable tool in extracting a more accurate meaning from unstructured texts. Ultimately, as WGPA combines both symbolic and sequential representations of information, it is believed to possess a high degree of applicability in various domains. A modified version of the Hellinger-Froessel-Neumann variational inequality, originally developed for hydrogen in a parabolic setting, has been established for rigid modes in glaciology and rigid layers. Contrary to the original HFN, our updated inequality involves a semi-definite velocity gradient constraint, making its study within a quadratic fourteenth-order elliptic operator context more challenging. Due to the lack of a finite-dimensional solution, we cannot employ the original HFN techniques, leading to the implementation of a novel method involving the use of rigid modes derived from the Lur\'e-Tarboule transform to restrict the velocity gradient to a finite-dimensional space for the purpose of proving and simplifying the modified HFN inequality. Additionally, we utilize this modification to address the so-called rigid modes problem in glaciology and rigid layers. As a byproduct of our study, we derive simplified versions of the HFN inequality, first, by assuming a compact velocity gradient, and second, by assuming that the rigid modes' energy density is infinitely differentiated. We further utilize our study to provide implicit bounds on the rigid modes' energy density. A generalization to the case of stationary incompressible ideal fluid also applies to the case of small electromagnetic perturbations in the presence of stationary incompressible electromagnetic flow. We establish that our findings conform with existing results, and a notable outcome of our study is the explicit determination of the modified HFN inequality, first, when the velocity gradient is a skew-Hermitian matrix, second, when the velocity gradient is a Hermitian matrix, and third, when the velocity gradient constraints are removed. We also derive a generalization to the case of stationary incompressible electromagnetic flow. Using ALMA and Chandra observations, we studied a set of 14 starburst galaxies, focusing on their molecular gas and energy emissions. The galaxies showed elevated star formation rates and metallicity, with a majority of their molecular gas expelled in massive outflows, typically moving at 400-1200 km/s. This expulsion was both cause and effect of the shortened gas lifetimes, though the exact relationship varied. The outflows were also creating shock fronts, with some casting a "bow-shock" shadow on the surrounding gas. The influence of the outflows on the gas was greater than that of the stellar feedback, with most of the gas being affected, though some regions, especially near the centers, were not, likely due to being contained by a central disc. The outflows were not having the desired effect of stopping the star formation, but rather accelerating it, by providing a mechanism for removing gas that made regions more susceptible to collapse. The expelled gas was also moving to surrounding halos, with velocities of 500-1000 km/s, and could potentially be contributing to the buildup of large halos, though further research is needed to confirm this. The outflows were also reducing the efficiency of the star formation, with an average efficiency of 1-2 solar masses per 10^9 solar masses, an order of magnitude lower than expected. The views of the shock fronts were typically offset from the views of the ionized gas, with some suggesting the ionized gas was not directly visible, and that the shock fronts were not creating significant amounts of ionized gas. This paper investigates the uniqueness problem for log-harmonic functions with prescribed real or complex singularities on the unit disk. Specifically, it asks whether such functions are determined by their values on the unit disk, given fixed real or complex singularities at a specific point. An efficient algorithm to compute Kendall's tau has a runtime of O(n^2) in expectation, where n is the number of observations in a dataset. To determine this algorithm's reliability, we establish that its expected discrepancy from the actual value of Kendall's tau remains within a certain range of values, specifically between -cn^2 and cn^2, where c is a constant and n is the number of observations in a dataset. In fact, we find that c=0.81 is a reasonable estimate for the constant c in our reliability bound, which means the discrepancy does not exceed cn^2 for some constant c and n times the square of the number of observations in a dataset. Furthermore, we also develop a theoretical bound on the discrepancy, expressed as cn^2, and compare its tightness by analyzing the constant c in our bound. In an extension of our findings, we also discover that an efficient modification of this algorithm allows for the accurate computation of various other rank-based statistics, such as Hirschfeld-Mann, Robinson, and Spearman's nonparametric forms. In these other cases, the expected discrepancy remains within -cn^2 and cn^2, where n is the number of observations in a dataset. As an additional contribution, we also develop a straightforward, deterministic method for computing Kendall's tau in a reliable manner. In comparison to the efficient algorithm, our reliable method has a substantially higher computational cost, specifically, it has an exponential complexity of 2^n. Yet, our straightforward, deterministic method precisely matches the statistical accuracy of the efficient algorithm, meaning both yield the exact same value of Kendall's tau in all cases. In an experimental assessment, we compared the performance of the efficient algorithm, the straightforward, deterministic method, and Burbea and Rao's (1985) approach for computing Kendall's tau in various datasets. Interestingly, our results revealed that the efficient algorithm, our straightforward, deterministic method, and Burbea and Rao's approach have an almost identical statistical accuracy, with only infrequent, sporadic instances of minor discrepancies. In general, these discrepancies occurred when the algorithms computed different signs for Kendall's tau, which does not necessarily indicate an issue, as the sign of Kendall's tau can be ambiguous in certain cases. In all cases where the algorithms computed different signs, we discovered that the difference could be attributed to a minor discrepancy, specifically, both algorithms computed values with opposite signs but one had a slightly higher absolute value, which is technically an error according to our definition of the expected discrepancy. A new approach to full pivot methods for linear programming, dubbed the facet pivot method, is presented and analyzed. This method mirrors the essence of Bland's vertex pivot but substitutes vertices with parallel faces as pivot elements. It is claimed that this method retains the same worst-case performance as Bland's algorithm but enjoys a more desirable average performance, courtesy of Monte-Carlo simulations. An intuitive explanation for the improved average performance is also provided. Interestingly, the proposed method can be integrated with interior point methods, such as the ellipsoid method, to yield a more efficient algorithm. Monte-Carlo simulations not only demonstrate the average performance but also how the balance between vertices and facets shifts during the iteration process. These simulations reveal that the balance favors faces in difficult instances and favors vertices in instances with easily identifiable optimal solutions or stations ary points. A modification to the ellipsoid method is presented that leverages the versatility of the facet pivot, resulting in a more ellipsoidal contour and potentially greater average efficiency. An open question regarding the statistical nature of the observed improvement in average performance was identified, suggesting room for further research. An alternative explanation for the improved average performance based on the average distance between the current solution and parallel faces was also proposed, which may hold greater significance than the Monte-Carlo simulations. Furthermore, the proposed pivot method was compared to auto-basis change, which was applied to Bland's algorithm, and surprisingly yielded comparable performance, despite boasting a more reliable average performance. An updated version of the auto-balance method, which accommodates parallel faces as pivot elements, was also presented and demonstrated. An implementation of the facet pivot method, coupled with auto-balance, was successfully integrated into IBM's LP solver, commonly known as MPSX, popular among practitioners. In parallel evolutionary algorithms, a system consisting of multiple populations operating in parallel is employed to tackle complex optimization problems.  However, there currently lacks a systematic approach to analyzing how search progress is conveyed between populations and shared effectively among the system as a whole.  We hypothesize that by merging insights from multigrid optimization algorithms and entropy reduction, leading to the introduction of a novel parent selection method,  filling this theoretical gap may be possible.  This method is designed to monitor and optimize the total entropic search progress of the system, contributing to a deeper understanding of system architecture and operation, as well as potentially boosting parallel evolutionary algorithm performance.  To test its efficacy, we employed our parent selection method in a series of application-based numerical optimization experiments.  These tests revealed the method to be beneficial and yielded superior results in the majority of cases when compared to conventional parallel evolutionary algorithms.  We conclude that our parallel evolutionary algorithm is more efficient and accurate, with these findings being backed by comprehensive statistical analysis.  Additionally, we were able to identify key insights into the method's operation, including its behavior at different population sizes, as well as how it influences parallel evolutionary algorithm performance and accuracy.  Notably, our method was found to be relatively fast and computationally frugal.  This study highlights the method as a powerful tool, capable of enhancing parallel evolutionary algorithm performance, as well as providing valuable insights into their operation.  We envision these findings to have a significant impact on the development and refinement of parallel evolutionary algorithms, contributing to a broader range of applications and applications of greater complexity and variability.  Additionally, we offer suggestions for how to tailor our parent selection method to specific parallel evolutionary algorithm applications.  Finally, we speculate on the potential future applications and realms of application of parallel evolutionary algorithms. We present the discovery of HINSA (Half-Period Emission Waveforms) in the C$^{18}$O($J=3-2$) molecule in the giant molecular cloud G176.51+00.20 through 119 $\mu$m. Spectro images reveal the presence of HINSA in the cloud's central region, where HCN and CO are, except for an isolated position near the cloud's edge. HINSA's ($\Delta$V$_{1/2}$) full width at half maximum varies from 0.11 to 0.25 km/s as the observation beam changes. As the cloud's velocity increases, HINSA's abundance generally decreases. Nevertheless, two areas with increased HINSA abundance relative to C$^{18}$O are found, associated with regions that have undergone enhanced gas friction and have low CO abundance. HINSA's ratio to the $^{13}$CO($J=3-2$) optical depth also reveals the presence of slowly rotating, turbulent gas within the cloud's interior. Conversely, the cloud's edge area is characterized by increased gas friction and decreased HINSA relative to $^{13}$CO($J=3-2$). It is suggested that HINSA's uniqueness stems from its ability to be generated through orbital angular momentum transfer to the gas within a rotating structure, such as a protostar or a spiral arm. Furthermore, the comparison with predictions made by the orbital angular momentum model indicates a need to consider the thermal broadening and line shape that originates from the transfer of angular momentum and to incorporate the effects of non-uniform gas distribution correctly. Such improvements would facilitate a more accurate understanding of HINSA's generation and distribution. The distribution of HINSA in the G176.51+00.20 cloud may serve as an indicator of which structures possess orbital angular momentum. Further investigation of HINSA is required to confirm its origin from orbital angular momentum. The challenge of changing image contexts between training and testing is a key obstacle for widespread image classification adoption. To overcome this, supervised domain adaptation techniques have been developed but often require extensive labeled data, making them impractical. In response, researchers have turned to unsupervised domain adaptation methods, including adversarial training, semantic transfer, and contrastive learning, which can learn valuable representations across different domains. By applying these methods to a reduced set of labeled data, it is possible to extend their usefulness to unrelated datasets, simplifying classification tasks in the process. The following paper explores how adversarial training, self-supervised learning, and semi-supervised learning can be used together to achieve cross-domain performance. The researchers present a novel cross-domain learning approach known as Semi-Syn, which uses a semi-supervised training method to create knowledge based on label correlations and combines this with self-supervised learning and semantic transfer for robust performance across different domains. The proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by significantly improving the accuracy of target predictions using only a small set of labeled images in the target domain, as demonstrated in experiments across three key visual recognition tasks. The results show that Semi-Syn achieves significantly higher target accuracy than current best approaches while also resulting in a more stable network that performs competitively on a fully unsupervised test. The end result is a network that outperforms all other approaches and offers a robust and reliable solution for cross-domain learning. The researchers also present a visual explanation of Semi-Syn's effectiveness that reveals its ability to create a more robust and stable representation than current approaches, effectively synthesizing data in the target domain to perform well at classification tasks. The approach opens up a range of applications for cross-domain learning and could be easily integrated into neural networks to extend their domain and improve classification task performance. The following paper presents the approach in detail, showcasing its effectiveness across three key visual recognition tasks, including fine-grained image classification across different domains, single-label multi-domain fine-grained image classification, and domain generalization in the context of zero-shot target classification. The approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in all tested contexts, significantly improving single-label target accuracy while also resulting in a more robust and stable network. The results open up a range of applications for cross-domain learning and provides a framework for understanding and analyzing neural network behavior in the process. The following paper presents the approach and dataset in detail, with all dataset images and code available online for future research. Understanding the underlying workings of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) everywhere possible is crucial, yet providing explanations is an incredibly difficult task due to their inherent complexity and diversity in architecture and data. There has been an emphasis on developing a method that effectively explains the relationship between input data and output predictions, while also accommodating a diverse array of GNN models and data types. Unfortunately, many existing methods are either too rigid, too time-consuming, or too burdensome to utilize in real-world scenarios. To counter this, we have created PGExplainer, an explainable AI approach that generates explanations through the use of perturbation-based gradient mapping. By formulating explanations as modifications to the original input graph, PGExplainer employs a diverse array of GNN models, numerous types of nodes, and multiple edge relations. Unlike other methods, PGExplainer can handle complex combinations of node and edge perturbations, resulting in explanations that are both accurate and straightforward. Our approach is as follows: we first utilize backpropagation to compute the gradient of a GNN's predictive output with respect to the original input graph. By optimizing this gradient via perturbation-based graph modification, PGExplainer generates explanations in the form of edited input graphs. Our thorough evaluation of explanations generated by PGExplainer reveals that our method delivers superior performance when measured by various factors, such as explanation fidelity, evidence quality, and overall clarity. Furthermore, PGExplainer significantly reduces the time required to generate human-friendly explanations containing a single node or edge relation. To facilitate widespread usage, we have developed a highly scalable Python framework called PGExplainer that incorporates multiple pre-trained GNN models, allowing for seamless integration with diverse types of nodes, edges, and machine learning algorithms. This framework also enables users to provide custom-defined node and edge features, thereby accommodating a broad spectrum of applications. PGExplainer is available for free at https://github.com/quantifyinglife/PGExplainer. Our investigation into the underlying factors driving explanation fidelity reveals that our method successfully identifies the most significant node and edge relations shared across multiple explanations, while also demonstrating the feasibility of using PGExplainer to provide a deeper understanding of the role of confounding variables in decision-making processes. Given its inherent versatility and scalability, we strongly believe that PGExplainer significantly contributes to the advancement of accurate and transparent explanations for GNN models. A Little Man Computer (LMC) architecture called Little Man Umachine (Umachine) was introduced in 1993 as a didactic machine for teaching computer fundamentals and programming to students. It utilized a 16-bit word size and supported floating-point operations through the incorporation of a memory component. A revamped version of Umachine, called Little Man Umachine with additional memory (UMU), was created and explored. UMU was created by expanding Umachine's memory component to accommodate a variety of deep learning algorithms, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. It was discovered that UMU could perform CNN model training at a speed of 0.021 seconds per iteration, while its performance and speed in Umachine ranged from 0.021 to 0.400 seconds. Furthermore, UMU's asymptotic training time for Umachine-based LSTM models with three hidden layers was $2.43 \times 10^4$ seconds, compared to the UMU-trained LSTM model's 562.16 seconds. Consequently, UMU's additional memory component enables it to perform and train more sophisticated neural networks faster and with greater efficiency. By simulating UMU on a variety of computers, researchers found that its assembly code variations achieved the highest speed, ranging from 19.8 million instructions per second to 125 million instructions per second. It was observed that UMU's performance using a Raspberry Pi 4 model 4 STB computer was 125 million instructions per second. These results demonstrate that UMU can be used for a variety of applications, including classification, image processing, and machine learning algorithm development, on a variety of computers. It was found that UMU's Umachine-based LSTM model achieved a accuracy of 67.71 percent in predicting random data. In contrast, training a three-layered LSTM model on genuinely random data using the UMU took 562.16 seconds and reached a 0.001 percent accuracy. Understanding the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe and the structure of the Standard Model of particle physics is the primary focus of ongoing and future particle physics experiments. These programs, driven by various motivations, also address other fundamental questions in physics. The dynamics of the Standard Model, in particular, can be explored through a few key variables, with a complex interplay between various energy scales being a key challenge. The Higgs boson's properties and the dynamics of the top quark, studied at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), are crucial in understanding the dynamics of the Standard Model. The CERN LHC's current and future experiments, alongside B-physics experiments, are ideally positioned to investigate the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry and initiate research into B beyond the Standard Model. The CERN Physics Programme is, for the most part, aligned with, while also reflecting to address, the 'Questions and Challenges for Particle Physics' outlined by the 2013 report from CERN's Future Programme Expert Committee. This report reviews the matter-antimatter asymmetry problem, reviewing its origins and presenting a simplified model of its development. It then describes the relevant aspect of current experiments and future facilities and apparatus, and finally discusses possible future research approaches. The review is primarily based on introductory lectures given to physicists working on the CERN Physics Programme, with the aim of aligning the various efforts under a unified set of goals and questions. While reviewing the matter-antimatter asymmetry problem might seem an 'external' task compared to the main focus of CERN's programmes, it is argued that this problem's intrinsic complexity and the required experimental approaches perfectly mirror the challenges faced by the researchers working on the programmes, thus making it an apt set of questions to guide the work. The impact of migration on languages is a complex issue that has garnered relatively little attention in mathematical modeling compared to other factors such as linguistic splitting and mergers. In this study, a basic model of migration influenced by demographic events is developed and analyzed using probabilistic methods. To tackle the challenge of dealing with a large number of populations moving across various geographical boundaries, a method for approximating the long-term language divergence process is established. Key outcomes of this investigation reveal that migration has the greatest effect during the early stages of the process and that the direction and intensity of migration influence can lead to significantly diverse outcomes. Consequently, several distinct scenarios of language evolution are conceivable. In one such scenario, a significant migration event can initiate a profound alteration in the direction of language divergence. In yet another scenario, a substantial difference in the intensity of migration influence can arise from the differing levels of migration intensity between various populations. It is also shown that there exists yet another possibility where a substantial difference in the direction of language divergence can emerge, though only under the hypothetical assumption that a substantial difference in the intensity of migration influence exists. To facilitate a deeper comprehension and visualization of these complex outcomes, various illustrative examples and case studies are presented at the end of this study. These case studies reveal that the model's predictions align with several historical examples of language divergence. Nonetheless, the model fails to adequately capture the essence of yet another case study. In particular, the model developed in this study is unable to account for the observed fact that English is not indicated as undergoing a significant change in the direction of language divergence. Possible explanations for this discrepancy are presented towards the end of this study. To facilitate a deeper understanding and visualization of these complex outcomes, several graphical illustrations of the long-term language divergence process are presented throughout this study.
