This study proposes a novel method for approximating an information metric, the mutual information $I(X;Y)$, that relies on characterizing the statistical properties of random variables $X$ and $Y$ through their moments. Utilizing the central moment expansion, we develop a formula linking the central moments of $X$ and $Y$ to the entries of the Karhunen-Loeve transform of their joint probability density function. This enables us to generate an expansion for the mutual information. By incorporating an entropy estimation formula based on central moments, we devise a highly efficient estimator for $I(X;Y)$ that performs well even when using a single data sample. This estimator emerges from a probabilistic analysis and is confirmed through analyses of reliability and bias. Additionally, experiments demonstrate its ability to estimate mutual information in various scenarios. Notably, this approach can also be applied to derive moment-based estimators for conditional entropy, conditional mutual information, and joint entropy. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the proposed estimator outperforms existing alternatives. This method provides an innovative solution for approximating information metrics in scenarios where only partial statistical data is available. The study explores the relationship between the proposed estimator and Karhunen-Loeve transform-based feature extraction. It also highlights a paradox in estimating mutual information when there is little or no correlation between random variables $X$ and $Y$. The research indicates that the proposed estimator can reduce a longstanding issue related to previous estimators, which suffered from the "additivity anomaly" problem. The solution for the additivity anomaly emerges naturally from the derivation process. A (Java)-based implementation of the proposed method is also made available on GitHub, allowing it to accommodate probabilistic distributions with an infinite number of dimensions. The code can be easily adapted for other programming languages like C, C++, MATLAB, and R. Furthermore, the research provides a comparison between the proposed estimator and alternative methods for the case of Gaussian random variables. The study indicates that the performance of the proposed estimator is largely independent of the probability distribution of $X$ and $Y$. A mathematical representation of the proposed estimator for the special case of joint probability density functions with compact support is also provided. The research finds that the spectral expansion has advantages over central moment expansion. A comparison between these two expansion techniques is presented. The study shows that the proposed feature extraction technique can be viewed as a generalization of the PCA algorithm, which deals with random variables having a Gaussian distribution. A framework illustrating the relationship between the proposed feature extraction technique and PCA is presented

Suppose we're analyzing a set of time-series data where the cross-sectional dimension, denoted N, increases as the sample size, n, grows. We focus on finding the number of shared stochastic trends if the data follow a non-linear vector autoregression model with significant errors, characterized by heavy-tailed distributions, and we establish the consistency of our estimator under these conditions. We also demonstrate that a specific method for determining the number of shared stochastic trends, based on a spectral approach, performs well even when data are heavily skewed and the sample size changes frequently. This is an advancement over existing spectral methods, which often require constant sample sizes and well-behaved data. Additionally, we develop an alternative technique for estimating the number of common stochastic trends, based on splitting methods, and show its asymptotic equivalence to the spectral approach under specific assumptions. Finally, we simulate various scenarios to evaluate how the accuracy of the spectral method is affected by non-normal data and non-constant sample sizes. Specifically, we investigate how altering n and n's relationship with N, as well as the properties of certain error terms, impact the method's performance. This research is significant because it addresses a long-standing issue related to dynamic factor models and common stochastic trends in large datasets. To further explore these problems, a supplementary document containing additional proofs, mathematical analyses, and theoretical discussions is included. Given a few captured images from a single camera, we aim to generate a high-resolution, three-dimensional scene representation. Traditional methods learn the scene geometry from these images, but they often struggle when the views are sparse and the objects are in the background. To overcome this challenge, we introduce geometric constraints to integrate information across all available images, thus enhancing the learning of scene geometry and image appearance. To effectively utilize the sparse views, we introduce a novel ray representation, which reduces the complexity of learning and improves efficiency. Furthermore, we adopt a multi-scale approach to accommodate varying view spacings and compensate for missing views by integrating the ray features across all images, thereby rectifying the existing bias in traditional methods. To optimize the overall pipeline, we approximate the multi-scale ray reconstruction using a novel optimization method that combines image and ray features. Our proposed framework, spaLLiF, outperforms existing methods in all benchmark tests, showcasing its capability to handle complex scenes and sparse views efficiently. The framework combines learning of scene geometry and image appearance while leveraging geometric constraints to achieve state-of-the-art results. To enable the reproduction of our results, the source code and pre-trained models of spaLLiF are publicly available on https://github.com/FeiLi1997/spaLLiF. Moreover, the three-dimensional scenes and corresponding images used in our experiments can be accessed through https://github.com/FeiLi1997/spaLLiF_data.

Though primarily targeting dwarf stars, our investigation also considered systems comprising smaller stars. By the end of our analysis in 2020, we had discovered seven newly paired or multi-star systems, publicly accessible through the Washington Double Star Catalog. Furthermore, we updated the catalog with existing stellar multiple systems, including those observed using our facility, adding a total of 35 new entries. A significant solar jet originating from AR12404 on September 12, 2018, was observed in high-resolution extreme ultraviolet imagery, and its movement coincided with a type II radio burst detected by the Nancay H-Obseratoire. Utilizing the LOw Frequency Array, an interferometer, it was possible to track both the jet and the radio burst in real-time as they propagated through interplanetary space. By analyzing the radio burst's dispersion measure, the speed of the shock associated with the jet exceeded 1,000 km/s, while the jet itself moved at approximately 180 km/s. This suggests that the shock generated tremendous amounts of energy that accelerated electrons down the jet's structure, generating the radio burst as the shock wave propagated through the jet. This phenomenon is a strong indication of the two phenomena being interconnected. Finally, by using the radio burst's speed, it was determined that the shock wave originated from the jet when it was approximately 9.5 arcseconds long, indicating that the shock wave's speed exceeded that of the jet by over fifty times. This is consistent with earlier predictions of how the shock wave would propagate relative to the jet. We examine a broad class of two Higgs doublet models characterized by vague scalar preferences. This model remains relatively undetermined and offers a high degree of freedom in constructing viable scenarios. We focus on testing its implications at future colliders, specifically on $B$ meson hadronizations, lepton flavor violations, and Higgs interactions, utilizing the most up-to-date experimental data to derive universal constraints. Notably, our analysis reveals significant discrepancies between the model's predictions and experimental observations in several measurements, with strong expectations of detecting these discrepancies at future colliders. The task of discovering predictive variables from complex time-series data involves a considerable challenge, partly due to the inherent delay in the causal relationships involved. In causal prediction tasks, two key factors are usually prioritized: effectively utilizing the time-related information in the data and rapidly pinpointing the relevant variables, both to accelerate learning and minimize unnecessary variable adjustments. In this paper, we develop a novel, hybrid approach that combines deep learning networks and specialized tools for variable selection, designed to handle a broad class of discrete-valued causal prediction tasks. By integrating a relevance learning component into a graph neural network, our proposed method automatically assigns weights to variables to prioritize those most likely to be relevant, thus reducing unnecessary computations and speeding up learning. Our results show that this network can effectively model the data and accurately predict the outcomes using surrogate variables, and we demonstrate its capabilities on a complex task involving predicting gene interactions in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans based on temporal expression data. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of our method to general discrete-valued causal prediction tasks through theoretical analysis. Additionally, we conduct an extensive experimental comparison with a range of alternative algorithms, including deep networks, and successfully apply the identified relevant variables to a real-world prediction task. The code used in this research is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository https://github.com/ashishgupta2/TimeSeriesCausalPrediction. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of variable efficiency and prediction accuracy when compared with existing state-of-the-art algorithms. The substantial improvements in the predictive accuracy achieved using the top variables are notable, with our proposed method resulting in superior performance using only 7 variables, whereas the best alternative algorithm requires as many as 30 variables, despite offering similar accuracy. In particular, our proposed method enhances predictive accuracy by as much as 0.3 when using the top 16 variables, while also achieving faster learning, since fewer variables need to be adjusted. In federated learning, data from various sources is typically encrypted and compressed to facilitate training. This traditional approach can be seen as applying Differential Privacy (DP) through data compression, with the goal of preventing individual data points from being inferred. This paper reinterprets DP as a compression mechanism and proposes a two-stage training process: first, conventional compressed learning is performed, then DP is applied to derive a robust model that prioritizes learning on more informative tasks. This approach is theoretically analyzed and demonstrated with empirical results. Unlike comparative methods, our approach ensures that each participant keeps the same amount of data, thus not introducing inference risks. We show that our approach can train models on extremely sensitive data, for example, facial images. Facial expressions datasets like EMOPAK and CK+ contain sensitive information and are typically non-ID, yet accurately identifiable when not compressed. Our approach allows deriving robust models from these datasets that are more similar to each other, and significantly more accurate than individual models derived from compressed data in all three settings. Additionally, our approach yields the best balance of accuracy and privacy when combining local data compression with DP. This privacy enhancement positions our approach as a stronger deterrent against adversarial manipulation that prioritizes learning from participants providing more informative data. Code is available at https://github.com/quantnow/FedDP. This work marks a significant advancement in understanding and leveraging DP in the context of federated learning. Further scaling our approach to massive datasets with varying data distributions is recommended for future exploration. Lastly, our approach's implications for facial action unit classification and potential real-world applications are discussed. We show that deriving models from compressed data in certain scenarios can yield comparable results to deriving models from uncompressed data, which may have implications for privacy. For example, analyzing the facial expressions of patients with chronic pain through facial expressions datasets like HAPID, CK+ and EMOPAK may not reveal individual pain levels if the model is not precise enough, thus maintaining their privacy. We conclude that understanding and leveraging DP in the context of federated learning can lead to innovative applications and solutions that prioritize privacy while yielding valuable insights. As games evolve, players' knowledge and abilities typically expand, enabling them to perceive more sophisticated patterns and outcomes, however conventional metrics ignore past performance, overlooking historical achievements and neglecting potential biases in assessment. With time-sensitive games where decisions influence future states significantly, utilizing past data to analyze skill levels is beneficial. A study focusing on a time-based, multi-player game - Skritt - is conducted to examine how players modify their understanding of game dynamics over time. By developing custom metrics for evaluating players' situational knowledge and understanding of game strategies, the research demonstrates that players develop familiarity with game mechanics at varying paces. Analysis shows that higher-level players tend to grasp more intricate game aspects compared to lower-level players, and understanding of game strategies correlates positively with skill level. Notably, when players encounter uncommon game states, they tend to struggle to identify these situations, and understanding of game strategies is a strong indicator of overall skill level, highlighting the value of backward-looking analysis in understanding player progression. This research provides novel insights into a well-established game, underscoring the significance of considering players' historical performance in analyzing skill levels. Furthermore, the study offers implications for researchers, game developers, and publishers by revealing valuable information about their target audience, thereby facilitating more accurate assessments and supportive environments for all players across various skill levels. The growing user base of apps on the App Store and Google Play Markets ensures a steady and consistent supply of mobile apps, enabling extensive research on completed tasks via user responses. Building upon the existing work of NetEase's research team, this paper focuses on population prediction problems, an essential component of many tasks such as recommendation systems, algorithm optimization, and population prediction itself. We introduce a novel method of estimated footprint area ratio (FEAR) that classifies users into two groups: those with large installed package count and those with small installed package count. We propose a new framework, consisting of two core features: publicly available characteristics, inherited from previous work, and our FEAR model, utilizing a Bayesian Threshold Gradient Boosting Machine as the core learning algorithm. Through experiments conducted on 16 population prediction tasks across various domains, our FEAR approach demonstrated superior performance, enhancing prediction accuracy by 9% compared to the baseline. Notably, FEAR's efficacy is most pronounced when compared to instances where only publicly available characteristics are lacking. We observed that our FEAR model consistently outperformed previous work on all population prediction tasks across multiple domains. We further analyzed the robustness of our FEAR model and discovered that its robustness is primarily attributed to the user group with small installed package counts. Given its exceptional performance and robustness, our FEAR model holds great potential for widespread application in industry and academia. With the continuous growth of mobile apps, population prediction is expected to experience significant advancements in the near future. This research introduces two innovative methods for constructing and applying static filters based on frequency and partitioning techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our solutions using real-world workloads and real-world data, showing them outperforming bitvector filters across various metrics. This pendulum model allows for in-depth analyses of well-known instability phenomena, which occur when the atom-molecule conversion begins, as well as Elsasser-like phenomena related to frequency mode coupling. Notably, although our approach is rooted in a quantum description, it offers a clear, self-consistent explanation for the emergence of these phenomena, which have previously been described mainly through qualitative interpretations of quantum statistics. To validate our approach, we compared the predicted behavior of our pendulum model with that of an actual BEC experiment. Our findings demonstrate that the simple, rigid pendulum can replicate the majority of the quantum condensate's dynamics features, but only under specific conditions. Specifically, we discovered a notable deviation in the single-frequency mode of the quantum pendulum's frequency, which is predicted by the effective pendulum model to be -1.053 times the frequency of the free quantum pendulum. Additionally, we observed another deviation in the single-frequency mode's asymmetry, which is predicted by the effective pendulum model to be -0.03151, in contrast to the asymptotic value of -0.027. These discrepancies suggest that the single rigid pendulum, although effective for qualitative analyses, may not be reliable for analyzing the quantum condensate's dynamics, particularly in cases where precise accuracy is essential. By applying the effective pendulum model with a stiffness consistent with the elastically coupled BEC, we have found that the single pendulum can accurately replicate the single frequency mode's frequency, as well as other key characteristics, including frequency mode coupling and atom-molecule population ratio. Notably, although our approach effectively replicates qualitative phenomena, it fails to reproduce the single pendulum's single frequency mode frequency when operating in the non-rigid state. Instead, we found that the single pendulum's frequency exhibits a single-frequency mode frequency, as well as other counterintuitive characteristics, such as negative frequency mode coupling. A quasi-compressible multi-phase version of the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method has been developed to address high-density ratio issues in two-phase simulations. By introducing a mass-dependent compressibility factor, we effectively resolve voids and phase separation problems. Additionally, we've incorporated thermodynamic equilibrium conditions for vapor-liquid phases and incorporated the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to model phase transition at specific temperatures and pressures. The proposed multi-phase SPH framework has been tested across a range of scenarios including void-taper problems, phase separation, and heat transfer between phases. The incorporation of quasi-compressibility improves mass conservation, eliminates voids, and enhances phase separation accuracy, reducing artificial viscosity. Furthermore, we've developed an original SPH-based method for simulating phase transition based on thermodynamic equilibrium, showing accurate results at specific temperatures and pressures. To address issues related to vapor-liquid phase transitions, we've developed an original heat conduction model, which effectively models convective heat flow between phases, as seen in the thermodynamic equilibrium test. The incorporation of both the thermodynamic equilibrium condition and the Clausius-Clapeyron equation ensures accurate results for one-phase and two-phase vapor-liquid phase transition scenarios. Overall, our multi-phase SPH framework has been thoroughly tested across a range of scenarios, demonstrating superior performance and accuracy compared to standard SPH methodologies. The developed framework provides a solid foundation for simulating multi-phase flows and thermodynamic processes in engineering applications. As such, it may be effectively utilized in a variety of scenarios including boiling processes, cooling systems, and phase transition simulations in two-phase flows. Future research could potentially incorporate thermal relaxation processes by extending the multi-phase SPH framework. Specifically, the number of operations required to update centroid estimates and calculate squared distances in each iteration is proportional to the number of data points, rather than the square of that value. (2) We've achieved similar results with K-means++. Both algorithms were outperformed by our approach in terms of clustering accuracy and runtime. Moreover, our results show that the centroid estimation and distance calculation routines in our algorithm are nearly optimal, utilizing nearly the minimum number of operations feasible on a quantum computer. This research compares two mathematical models that use a hierarchical approach to describe how plants grow in response to varying nitrogen soil levels. By applying these models, a statistical method for estimating unknown parameters based on experimental data is developed. Key parameters that characterize each model can be thought of as an internal and an external control point, respectively, where the internal control point determines a plant's potential size, while the external control point determines size across an entire population. To illustrate the effectiveness of this new statistical method, it is applied to measurements of corn plant sizes in two different nitrogen soil experiments. 

Notably, this method reveals a significant positive relationship between the external control point and nitrogen soil levels in one experiment, but no such relationship exists in the other experiment. In experiment settings where corn plants are rotated regularly, it's observed that only those in the outer portion tend to grow larger in response to increasing nitrogen soil levels, whereas those in the inner portion display no such growth. This phenomenon is not captured by the first mathematical model, but is predicted by the second one. Consequently, it can be concluded that the first mathematical model is more appropriate for describing the results of these two specific experiments. 

This comparative study highlights the need for researchers to carefully choose which mathematical model is most suitable for a particular set of experimental data, thus contributing to our understanding of the interplay between the environment and an organism's size. To achieve this, we propose an automated method aimed at selecting the optimal mathematical model by evaluating which one yields the lowest residuals between predicted and actual sizes, or, alternatively, the lowest mean squared standard errors. Moreover, based on the analysis of experimental data, it's estimated that the potential size, or maximum corn size, is approximately 13.4 cm when grown in the highest amount of nitrogen, or 15.4 N. Additionally, it's estimated that the size of corn plants in the outer portion, or 12 N, is around 8.4 cm on average. The transport properties of a carbon nanotube film at high temperatures were examined using a four-terminal measurement setup that used graphene contacts. The current-voltage characteristics displayed voltage-independent resistance in the range of 300 to 700 K. However, below 250 K, the resistance started to fluctuate in a periodic manner and exhibited a correlation with temperature, resulting in increased resistance as the temperature decreased. Using four-terminal measurements helped distinguish between contact and nanotube contributions to the resistance, revealing that the resistance primarily stems from the nanotubes. The observed resistance can be attributed to a percolation mechanism that occurs among the nanotubes, which are aligned perpendicular to each other, allowing for the easy transfer of carriers between them. The resulting quantum percolation network explains the nanotube film's electrical properties, which can be further modified by adding bridges to the system to create a quantum tunneling effect. The bridge formation, which can be triggered by applying a higher bias than the nanotube film's work function, allows for the observation of a plateau in the current-voltage characteristics. The width of this plateau depends on the density of the nanotubes and can be used to determine the threshold bias required to create the tunneling bridges. The quantum tunneling effect can also be confirmed by examining the temperature dependence of the nanotube film's resistance. The experiment found that the nanotube film's resistance exhibits thermally activated behavior when the temperature is below 400 K and the bias is sufficiently high. The observed activation energy can be used to calculate the average length of the tunneling bridges. The quantum tunneling effect helps to explain the remarkable stability of the carbon nanotube film's electrical properties over time and temperature. The ability to control the quantum tunneling effect by adjusting the bias also allows for the nanotube film's conductivity to be fine-tuned. The method used to create the tunneling bridges, which relies on a percolation mechanism, is distinct from the chemical modification approach used in previous studies. The development of tunneling bridges within carbon nanotube films offers a potential method to control the room temperature bipolar resistive memories and creates new opportunities for the development of carbon nanotube-based electronic devices. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the benefits of combining carbon nanotubes with graphene to create stable and flexible carbon nanotube film devices. Overall, the success of AMoE highlights its effectiveness in tuning the MoE model's parameters, accurately mapping to the dataset, and generalizing to unseen data. Experimental outcomes suggest that the new approach can also be applied to other neural network architectures. We've developed a new approach for breaking global symmetries by gravity in a specific type of quantum gravity theory based on a spin foam model. This model incorporates an element called kinematic non-abiding, which suggests that quantum states can be entangled with a spacetime region that violates the original global symmetry. By applying an adapted version of the volume operator from spin foam quantum gravity, we've been able to derive an expression for the breaking of symmetry by gravity. As a result, we've set the stage for empirical testing of certain theoretical predictions that go beyond standard lore, including the possibility that gravity may not violate time reversal symmetry and the presence of specific gravitational anomalies. Moreover, our findings imply a lower bound on how much gravity can disrupt spacetime. This lower bound is significant, amounting to at least $10^{-18}$G, which is comparable to current laboratory capabilities, albeit with some limitations. Finally, our analysis has implications for other quantum gravity theories, including loop quantum gravity, leading to distinct differences in how these theories predict the behavior of gravity. By contrast, breaking global symmetries by gravity in loop quantum gravity appears to be in line with expectations based on classical general relativity, whereas the same phenomenon in spin foam quantum gravity suggests significant deviations. This difference in predictions could potentially be tested using upcoming table-top experiments in the area of gravitational physics. Multi-modal models that incorporate knowledge, such as object categories, spatial relationships, and semantic meanings, have improved the resilience of learning systems. To maximum this potential, we create a novel knowledge model that utilizes external knowledge and adjusts it dynamically to suit the requirements of the learning task. To achieve this, we introduce a federal learning framework that allows a central authority to manage a decentralized learning network consisting of multiple parametric models. This framework empowers the central authority to adjust the importance of each model, which in turn, enables a dynamic distribution of training data among the parametric models based on their respective task performances. Furthermore, we develop a federal batch normalization method that enhances model diversity and resilience by promoting a federal consensus among the parametric models. Comprehensive experiments conducted on multi-modal, semi-supervised, domain adaptive, and black box adversarial robustness tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed federal learning framework and federal batch normalization method. Notably, our federal learning framework and methods consistently outperform existing federal and decentralized learning frameworks on all tested tasks, often by a margin of significant improvement. For instance, our federal learning framework and methods achieve a significant 9.5% improvement over state-of-the-art models on a particular semi-supervised learning task while reducing model diversity. This means that, instead of analyzing data sequences in the order they occur, it looks back at previous values to identify long-term patterns. This backward approach enables significant reductions in data sequence length by efficiently encoding repeated patterns. However, when dealing with datasets that contain uniform data, the BDA algorithm actually ends up increasing the overall file size due to a theoretical flaw in the original concept. This raised an important validity question - can a modified version of the BDA algorithm effectively compress uniform data while maintaining its ability to compress sequences effectively. Our research involves designing an enhanced variant of the BDA algorithm by using a measurement tool to gauge data sequence changes and only looking back at parts of the sequence that show significant variations. Using the Backward Dropping Algorithm with the Temporal Reference Pointer, we tested various threshold values to see how this new approach impacts compression performance. The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules is considered natural due to their underlying QCD forces, which are strong enough to hold them together. In contrast, the existence of di-atomic molecules composed of two heavy particles, however, poses a challenge within the conventional framework of QCD. This is because such molecules, if they were to exist, would facilitate a process that violates the conservation of quark flavor, which is not typically allowed under QCD principles. In the context of charm quarks, for instance, this would involve two heavy quarks being bound together in a molecule, only to be split apart and reconfigured as different quarks in another bound state. In contrast, theories like Regge Kaluza-Klein models, which allow for such transformations, are considered exotic and unlikely to describe the actual situation. We explore here the possibility that such heavy-hadronic molecules could be used as platforms to study exotic states not yet observed, which are predicted to appear near thresholds where bound and continuous states with the same properties meet. We specifically examine two potential test cases: a di-atomic $D^{\ast}$-meson molecule and a di-atomic $\Upsilon$-meson molecule, which could be detected with the aid of a laser interferometer. Such an instrument is planned for space deployment in the LISA observatory, which is currently being constructed to study gravitational waves. In the case of the $D^{\ast}$-meson molecule, simulations indicate that its characteristics would allow for unambiguous identification using LHCb's experimental setup, which is capable of detecting particles containing charm. In the case of the $\Upsilon$-meson molecule, simulations predict that its detection would be within the capabilities of the upcoming BESIII experiment, which is specifically designed for particle-collisions involving bottom quarks. In both scenarios, analysis of particle interactions near thresholds would provide insights into the underlying dynamics of heavy-hadronic molecules and potentially reveal information about unusual states not yet observed. In the process, this would resolve whether these molecules exist in a state of bound continuity and whether they can be used to study unusual states with similar properties. The concept of swarm robotics has been explored within the robotics community for some time, but a growing interest from military and industrial entities is starting to reveal a significant concern: civilian safety threats posed by autonomous military drones. As a result, a multi-faceted approach is being taken to address this issue, encompassing research, legislation, and technology-driven initiatives. Our paper delves into a comprehensive review of military drones and swarming technology, examining cutting-edge research, highlighting prominent countries and institutions involved, and outlining current standards and initiatives aimed at mitigating swarm-related threats. A discussion on potential future directions is also presented, including the role of civilian drones and counter-swarming measures. Our review reveals a striking disparity: the United States and China are at the forefront of military drone and swarm research, whereas other countries are relatively underrepresented. Additionally, a lack of transparency and public access to relevant Swarming Technology Data (STDT) is identified, predominantly available in the United States. Our findings are intended to provide valuable insights for government agencies, research institutions, and technology developers to better grasp the complexities and challenges associated with swarm threats. Furthermore, a call for action regarding data sharing and international collaboration is made, aiming to address this high-stakes issue. Our research proposes a swarm threat assessment model that enables near-real-time detection and analysis of potential threats in the United States. Inspired by AI-driven medical diagnostic tools, this model's performance in simulated scenarios reveals remarkable accuracy and latency capabilities. Our analysis reveals that by combining AI, time-series forecasting, and anomaly detection, the identification and tracking of swarm entities at a national and regional level can be significantly enhanced. A proposed national swarm threat alert system is also introduced, which can rapidly disseminate critical information to concerned parties. Our research contributes significant insights on swarm threat awareness, threat avoidance strategies, and potential counter-measures. A proposed framework for integrating drone swarms with the energy sector is also presented, designed to withstand advanced cyber attacks. Inspired by the resilience of the human immune system, this model's core principle is immunity. Our review reveals that current swarm computing and resource allocation approaches predominantly focus on traditional infrequent network situations, whereas dynamic flow control and games-inspired models offer more tailored solutions for today's shared network environments. Conversely, the review finds a significant lack of research on the sharing of Swarming Technology Data (STDT) for drone swarms. However, the United States is recognized as a leader in relevant STDT, with a proposed federal initiative aimed at collaborating international efforts being identified as a key opportunity for growth.

Youling, which means "predicting the steps of others" in a Chinese dialect, is a groundbreaking approach to zero-shot and multi-path pedestrian trajectory prediction. Current research in this field has several shortcomings: many methods require extensive data for fine-tuning, while concurrent approaches only predict single paths despite many pedestrians exiting multiple locations, and research involving real-world datasets like Cityscape has been limited. A novel framework called Youling addresses these issues by performing path prediction based on unmarked, annotated Cityscape without the need for additional data, and accurately forecasting multiple paths for each person. A self-supervised module called PLink is introduced that establishes inter-pedestrian connections over time. By doing so, PLink enables the model to discover movements that are characteristic to groups of people by producing a latent representation that involves the interactions between individuals. This facilitates the model's ability to produce multiple trajectory predictions for each person by assigning them to relevant groups. As a result, Youling outperforms other approaches on both Cityscape and SUNCG datasets, including path prediction and point-based forecasting. introduce a novel supervised segmentation and classification system, which

We propose a variational method to approximate the adiabatic gauge potential based on the dynamics of a quantum system coupled to a slow-changing external field, aiming to extend the Born-Oppenheimer approximation to highly degenerate cases. A key factor in this method involves the optimal choice of variational parameters, which are connected to the system's commutators and, specifically, the nested commutators of $A_0$ with itself and lower-order versions, in relation to the underlying Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$. We establish an explicit expression for these optimal parameters, stating they equal the squared Frobenius norms of these commutators, a relationship also applicable to other relevant operators. Furthermore, we analyze the method's convergence and determine an expression for its remaining error term. Additionally, we discuss a suitable configuration for the variational parameters and outline a method to iteratively improve the approximation, leading to the emergence of a new, geometric approximation for the adiabatic gauge potential, along with its own error estimate. We also extend the method to the case where the system's wave function is the eigenstate of a degenerate state, rather than the most stable one, by employing a version of the adiabatic gauge potential and associated error estimates. We provide an alternative characterization of the parameters connected to the nested commutators, along with a discussion of its relevance to the system's stability. Lastly, through the application of the method to the case of a degenerate particle in one-dimensional scenarios, we performed a detailed numerical comparison of the approximated adiabatic gauge potential with its exact version, confirming the theoretical convergence results. We have also obtained a quantitative analysis of the parameters connected to the nested commutators, as well as an approximation of the geometric error, in relation to specific, non-standard configurations. Furthermore, our research reveals that despite degeneracies that are not extremely pronounced, the system exhibits complex dynamics and substantial deviations from standard predictions occur. Lastly, our study demonstrates the potential for the derived approximation of the adiabatic gauge potential to contribute to the improvement of electron-phonon coupling models in scattering simulations.

An image simulation model based on wavelength-dependent image refraction was developed, taking into account varying optical refractive indices for different wavelengths and accounting for chromatic aberration effects. By comparing the simulated refractive properties of commercial lenses and scientific objectives, the significance of chromatic aberration is demonstrated. Furthermore, a perception distortion metric is introduced and assessed in a comprehensive study involving 48 subjects, which compares and discusses the effects of chromatic aberration and lateral chromatic aberration on image quality perception. The results reveal that chromatic aberration causes noticeable color distortions leading to image quality perception degradation, whereas lateral chromatic aberration generally has a minimal effect. Consequently, an adaptive optics system incorporating a continuous wavefront deformable liquid crystal panel is proposed for mitigating chromatic aberration effects by compensating for refractive index irregularities. An experimental validation of the proposed solution demonstrated its effectiveness in suppressing chromatic aberration effects, as verified using a point spread function analysis technique. Yukawa coupling couplings between Higgs bosons and fermions are fundamental components in the Standard Model. Although the couplings between Higgs bosons and quarks are challenging to test due to the small Yukawa coupling values, measurements are feasible with enhanced precision at the High Luminosity phase of the LHC. In contrast, light scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings are more easily detectable due to larger coupling values. This analysis examines the constraints on scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings in association with a Z boson using single top quark decays within the Standard Model and explores the potential to detect such processes at the LHC with data from 300 fb^-1 and 3000 fb^-1 data sets. Current constraints on CP-even and CP-odd couplings are compared, and the ability to combine data from the High Luminosity phase of the LHC is evaluated. Furthermore, the paper presents a comprehensive study on how accurately individual and combined couplings can be determined. Ultimately, the analysis examines the viability of detecting scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings in various processes at the LHC. Using a simplified model where a single right-handed vector or axial Yukawa coupling exists, the analysis determines that masses for vector couplings up to 1.4 GeV and axial couplings up to 0.65 GeV can be detected with high confidence. Importantly, the model reveals that light scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings can be directly excluded at LHC with high confidence. This analysis further reveals that light scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings can be used to test the anomaly between the Higgs boson decay rates to fermions and their respective Yukawa coupling values. This unexplored relationship opens the possibility for indirect detection of light scalar-Yukawa coupling couplings in various processes at the LHC. Lastly, the analysis examines the potential for the LHC to identify or exclude LHC light scalar-Yukawa coupling anomalies. Using a simplified model where a single right-handed vector or axial Yukawa coupling exists, the analysis determines that light scalar-Yukawa coupling masses can be identified or excluded between 0.1-40 GeV and 0.1-20 GeV, respectively, with high confidence. This research investigates the impact of diverse training data on the performance of speech recognition models in terms of robustness to speaker variation and topic shifts. Initially, we draw a distinction between the precision and reliability of speech recognition models. Precision is defined as the average performance across various topics, whereas reliability is measured as the probability that the model performs better than a baseline model for novel topics. To simulate the robustness of speech recognition models, we created multiple topic expansion scenarios with a central topic and surrounding topics, and controlled the similarity of these topics to the central one using three dimensions: speaker, semantic, and phonetic. We analyzed the effect of diverse training data on the precision and reliability of speech recognition models by varying the number of topic expansion instances. Furthermore, we conducted an experiment where a neural network was trained on data from multiple topics using an incremental learning protocol. The results showed that increasing diversity in training data improved the robustness of the model, as indicated by higher precision and reliability metrics. Interestingly, the metrics indicated that the model was more resistant to semantic topic expansions and less resilient to phonetic expansions. Additionally, the experiment demonstrated that incremental learning enhanced the model's precision and reliability for all three expansion types. Notably, the model trained on data from multiple topics and using incremental learning achieved the highest precision and reliability scores, observed for topic expansions by speaker, semantic, and phonetic types. Consequently, the results of this research establish diversity in training data as a robustness metric for speech recognition. Moreover, the results show that neural networks can achieve consistent performance on novel topics, thanks to the incremental learning protocol and diversity in training data. Finally, the research reveals that speaker diversity greatly affects the precision and reliability of speech recognition models, but the impact of semantic and phonetic diversity is more significant in certain scenarios. Overall, the results provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners on optimizing speech recognition systems in real-world applications. Furthermore, the research proposes new diversity metrics that can aid in the design of more robust speech recognition systems. Lastly, the results show that neural networks can achieve a baseline that diminishes with increasing distance between the central and expanded topics, and suggest that using predicted posteriors from a speaker classifier as weights in incremental learning may enhance model robustness. The research found that expanding topics by speaker provide the largest edge in terms of precision and reliability. Moreover, the results indicate that neural networks can achieve similar precision and reliability as speaker-based expansions when trained on data from semantic and phonetic topics. To apply image-text embeddings more widely, we focus on a new challenge, 
multi-domain image captioning. Current models perform best within their 
training data context, but we want a single model that works across all 
domains without needing to be trained on every domain individually. 
One way to achieve this is by using images and captions from other domains 
to augment the training data for our model, and we explore different 
techniques for doing this. By applying a style transfer method to images and 
creating synthetic training pairs across domains, we see significant 
improvement in performance, up to 4.3 points better than a model trained in 
its native domain alone. Additionally, by using these synthetic data points 
for few-shot learning, we see further performance gains, up to 12.4 points. 
This new approach means we can train a single model that performs well across 
all domains without being trained on every domain individually, saving 
considerable resources. Experiments are conducted across four distinct domains 
(from 1 to 20 styles) to test the effectiveness of this method. Further details 
can be found in our work titled "DomainMix: A Data augmentation approach to 
unify image captioning domains of various styles". The code and data are 
available on GitHub at https://github.com/dominiklcz/DomainMix.

The first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator, after normalization, can be represented as $\lambda_n = 2n$. This consideration led to a search for an optimal geometric setup that minimizes $\lambda_n$ for any given $n$. In this context, a modified Faber-Krahn type inequality was established. Furthermore, determining the optimal configuration proved equivalent to solving the isoperimetric problem in even-dimensional Euclidean space, with constraints imposed by the eigenvalue's degeneracy based on their corresponding quantum numbers. A numerical solution for the minimum value of $\lambda_n$ was obtained for multiple values of $n$. This result was verified by comparing it with the minimum value of the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian operator, both in the context of normalized operators and their unconstrained version. Ultimately, it was observed that the eigenvalues of the Laplacian are greater than those of the Hermite operator for all $n$. This phenomenon bears similarity to a previously established inequality by Borsuk. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset comprising 12 classes from CIFAR-10, the proposed method is capable of identifying instances that do not adhere to NTK's criteria. Experiments conducted on the NTK-based learning mechanism showcase that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing solutions in addressing biases. Our findings demonstrate that an NTK-based model, aided by the proposed framework, can learn faster, rely on fewer data points, and provide more intuitive explanations than a baseline ResNet model. The research's source code and data are publicly available. This work highlights an interesting paradox where a more complex model like CNNs can be surpassed by a simpler NTK-based model. The research's key contributions include a model-agnostic framework for diagnosing NTK, a framework for addressing model-specific biases, a framework for measuring a model's fairness, a comprehensive dataset comprising 12 classes from CIFAR-10, and a framework that makes NTK-based learning mechanisms more resource-efficient by reducing the required data storage and training complexity by approximately two orders of magnitude. The Hatano-Nelson chain, a non-Hermitian model with long-range correlations, has an unusual energy dispersion, characterized by complex poles. We investigated the consequences of extending this model by incorporating additional correlation, referred to as the $\beta$-$\gamma$ chain. Previous studies had shown that the Hermitian version of this model exhibits persistent correlations. Notably, in the non-Hermitian framework, the effect of these correlations on the skin effect becomes apparent only in the density of states. We discovered that the additional correlation introduces a minimum in the density of states at certain complex energies for the $\beta$-$\gamma$ chain. Furthermore, for weak non-Hermitian fluctuations, the density of states can be described using the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck theory, with the observed correlation resulting in a shift of the absorption band. We established a set of non-Hermitian models, including the $\beta$-$\gamma$ chain, whose density of states can be exactly determined using a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model-based Bethe lattice analysis. The resulting density of states contains a band and two picket-fence spectra, located at complex energies that are determined by the model parameters. We observed that the positions of the picket-fence spectra exhibit a linear dependence on the imaginary axis. Moreover, for certain parameter ranges, the resulting spectra exhibit a gap between the absorption band and the picket-fence spectra. We discovered that the distinct features of the density of states can be used to distinguish between different non-Hermitian models. We discussed the implications of the observed findings, including the effect of localized states on the resulting spectra, and the different characteristics of the electron transport in the non-Hermitian frameworks. The observed phenomena provide insights into the interplay between localization and delocalization in systems governed by non-Hermitian mechanics. Moreover, the applied models have potential applications in the study of quantum transport in systems with complete and incomplete transmission. In particular, the extended Hatano-Nelson chain may model the absorption of light in the presence of a mirror, while the $\beta$-$\gamma$ extended model can be used to describe the absorption of light in systems with high reflectivity, such as cat-eye materials. Furthermore, the models bear resemblance to non-Hermitian quantum graphs with long-range correlations, potentially facilitating their experimental implementation in, for instance, topological surface states of $d$-wave superconductors or photonic quantum graphs. The pion-nucleon sigma term (also known as the integrated, off-shell cross section for scattering pi N to N N) is essential but difficult to measure directly, which is why it's been estimated indirectly since the 1970s; more recent estimates have been made using chiral perturbation theory. A new method for calculating the sigma term has been developed from three-flavor chiral perturbation theory, which treats the masses of pions and kaons differently, and also makes assumptions about the role of lambda nucleons. A value for the total pion-nucleon sigma term was calculated as roughly 37 MeV, which is consistent with previous estimates, which suggests that a term for the strange mass may be unimportant. This finding could have a significant impact on nuclear physics because it shows that while the sigma term is connected to the scalar potential acting on nucleons and affecting nuclear depth and quark content, its value is sufficiently small that it will not significantly impact calculations based on chiral effective field theory. This is particularly true for calculations based on two-flavor theory, which may be a reasonable approximation given that current pion energies are significantly higher than kaon energies in nucleons; this means that two-flavor theory may work better than three-flavor theory and that the lambda nucleon's role may be sufficiently small that it can be considered negligible. A value for the strange pion-nucleon sigma term was also calculated as roughly -5 MeV, which is consistent with a previously estimated value of -4 MeV. A new method for calculating the sigma terms for the scattering of kaons and lambda nucleons was also developed, which is based on a theory that describes the strange physics of lambda nucleons. A large and negative value for the total strange sigma term was calculated as roughly -80 MeV. A new method for calculating the relative contributions to the sigma terms of quark masses and scalar potentials was also developed, which is based on a technique called the Feynman-Hellmann theorem, which shows that while the sigma terms are significantly affected by quark masses, they are not significantly affected by scalar potentials. This finding could have a significant impact on nuclear physics because it suggests that the sigma terms may be a poor measure of nuclear quark content. This is particularly true for calculations based on chiral effective field theory because if the sigma terms are dominated by quark masses, then this suggests that the theory may successfully explain the sigma terms without needing to consider the role of scalar potentials. This is the second paper in a series focusing on the relationship between a galaxy's environment and the presence of an active galactic nucleus (AGN). The study utilizes the GAMA near-infrared dataset to compare the characteristics of AGN host galaxies and non-AGN galaxies across multiple redshift intervals. To account for the potential AGN influence, we employed two methods: a pre-depletion analysis and a post-depletion correction using a machine learning algorithm. The findings reveal that the classification precision of AGN host galaxies and non-AGN galaxies exhibits a significant variation based on the redshift interval. At lower redshifts (up to z=0.2), AGN host galaxies tend to be less massive, whereas at higher redshifts (z>0.2), they exhibit greater or less star formation activity relative to non-AGN galaxies, presenting no consistent behavior. Moreover, using the pre-depletion method, we identify notable environmental characteristics, weight differences, and star formation activity patterns among AGN host galaxies relative to non-AGN galaxies, whereas the post-depletion method reveals a complex relationship between AGN contribution and galaxy mass and star formation rates. The study's results are consistent with the majority of previous findings, indicating that high-mass, star-forming galaxies are susceptible to AGN activation, whereas low-mass galaxies, especially those that are quenched, are more likely to host an AGN. The findings are in line with the galactic feedback theory, supporting a connection between an AGN and its host galaxy. The study's outcomes are heavily influenced by the chosen spectral analysis method and galaxy classification precision, underscoring the need for an unbiased evaluation, high-galaxy classification precision, and a more accurate AGN correction technique to explore the AGN relationship with its host galaxy. Our recent study discovered that adding synthetic predictors created using simple methods can improve the predictive accuracy of complex datasets controlled by underlying latent factors. The enhancements in predictive accuracy using the predictive model occur because the synthetic predictors synthesize information that was not utilized by the predictive model, thus refining its predictions. Conversely, when predictive models already utilize all the predictive information available, adding synthetic predictors yields diminished or no enhancements in predictive accuracy. The enhancements in predictive accuracy only persist if the predictive model remains stable in the enhanced feature space, which implies that the added predictors mimic the original features effectively. Consequently, we developed a stability metric that quantifies how well the predictive model adjusts to changes in the original features and how well it adjusts to changes in the synthetic predictors. The goal is to utilize these metrics as part of an automated process for selecting the optimal number and type of synthetic predictors to add to any given predictive model, which in turn can lead to novel methods for extracting features from data. The class of models we utilized for our study includes variational auto-encoders (VAE) but similar findings can also be observed in other models including linear models and graph convolutional networks. The findings from our study reveal the importance of a model's stability in determining its performance with added features and also reveal that enhancing predictive accuracy sometimes requires compromising some aspects of predictive precision. This research paper is centered on investigating warped product semi-slant submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds, as well as their pointwise semi-slant counterparts. We begin by identifying a classification of T-warped product semi-slant submanifolds within $\bar{\kappa}$-Sasakian manifolds, which are a specific type of Sasakian manifold. Furthermore, a theorem has been derived that provides necessary and sufficient conditions for a pointwise semi-slant submanifold to be a warped product. This has led to several consequences and generalizations of existing theorems, including those related to slant and semi-slant submanifolds in both Riemannian and Sasakian contexts. Crucially, our findings also imply that (semi-)slant warped product submanifolds are largely restricted to the torus $T^n$, with the exception of a specific case in $\bar{\kappa}$-Sasakian manifolds and another in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^{2n+m}$. Additionally, some open questions have been posed regarding non-existence cases in both Riemannian and Sasakian contexts. We are also able to contribute a broader, more comprehensive version of a previously existing theorem regarding slant submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds. This research is a direct extension of previous work by Montes, Garling, and many others. We have also taken the initiative to address the unknown cases of non-existence mentioned above, which holds potential for further exploration in the field. This research is an essential component in understanding warped product (semi-)slant submanifolds, with the ultimate goal of developing a comprehensive classification of such submanifolds. Various network stability measurements have been proposed in the last few years.
We've developed a new metric called Gromov centrality that evaluates an individual node's contribution to a network's overall cluster structure at multiple scales.
By applying different scaling factors, Gromov centrality allows us to distinguish between mesoscale and macroscale nodes, as well as nodes with high modularities and those situated between communities.
We've encountered both similarities and differences in the behaviors of various network types when analyzing Gromov centrality.
For example, in a political network, the metric identifies influential figures beyond the top-degree ones, whereas in a protein network, the primary interests are the interacting proteins themselves.
We've also compared Gromov centrality with other centrality measures using various networks and found that - in some cases, where a node participates in multiple communities - the metric can highlight key community members overlooked by others.
Based on these observations, we've developed the multi-scale community browser, a graphical user interface that utilizes Gromov centrality for visualizing and exploring community structures. 
By analyzing Gromov centrality, we've identified distinct patterns in various networks, such as a bimodal distribution of values in Facebook networks, and - in networks of articles and sentences - a power-law distribution of node centralities that closely resemble human expectations. 
These findings suggest that different network centrality measures can provide insights into unique aspects of a network. 
By analyzing these disparate indicators, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate structure of a network. 
In closing, the utility of Gromov centrality lies not only at the network level but also at the user interface level, where it enables users to explore community structures in networks beyond what is possible with current methods.

Recently proposed ADAPT-VQE algorithms, which combine the strengths of the Hamiltonian-based QEB method and variational quantum eigensolver, have shown superior performance in pre-optimization and post-optimization phases. Compared to its fermionic and qubit counterparts, the multi-reference ADAPT-VQE approaches the FCI method with optimal computational complexity, and by using a mixed basis it simultaneously achieves efficient wavefunction representation and optimal computational complexity. A modified qubit-ADAPT-VQC algorithm has also been introduced to locate the stationary points of the groundstate and excited states of highly correlated molecules efficiently. However, the proliferation of qubits necessitates the application of various narrow-range and wide-range compression techniques to realize efficient qubit-ADAPT-VQC algorithms. In this study, the qubit-ADAPT-VQC algorithm employing a two-step FQAS and FISW compression scheme was used in conjunction with the multi-reference ADAPT-VQE framework for ground and excited state calculations on molecules exhibiting strong static and dynamic correlations. The results reveal a significant reduction in computational cost with minimal loss in accuracy due to the combined effects of multi-reference description and qubit compression, resulting in an acceleration factor of approximately two compared to the fermionic-ADAPT-VQC and qubit-ADAPT-VPCID methods. In particular, the qubit-ADAPT-VQC algorithm with two-step FQAS and FISW compression achieved an accuracy of 99.99% for the total number of basis states and 99.97% for the total number of Pauli strings with a variable number of qubits and energy levels, depending on the molecule under study. In conclusion, the qubit-ADAPT-VQC approach presents a promising method for efficient ground and excited state calculations on molecules with strong static and dynamic correlations. The empirical results indicate the need to balance the trade-off between computational speed and accuracy in the design of efficient qubit quantum algorithms. A recent model called Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) aims to incorporate prior knowledge of a probability distribution by learning its inverse mapping from the data space to a representation space. When used with labeled data, the DGD can spontaneously derive a classification boundary, separating classes in the chosen representation space. However, the question remains whether the DGD can consistently identify the optimal classification model, given varying datasets drawn from the same data distribution. In this study, the DGD is defined as a specific type of inverse autoregressive network, for which the optimal learning model in the GMM context is established. Under these specific conditions, the results show that the DGD leads to consistent classification performance. A graphical representation illustrates how potential inconsistencies arise when moving from one-dimensional to multi-dimensional Gaussian mixtures. Experimental outcomes further validate the model's ability to achieve consistent classification performance. Additionally, the model analysis provides the basis for an efficient classification tool, which was tested on various labeled data sets and produces classification results competitive with current state-of-the-art models. In practical applications, the DGD can effectively incorporate prior knowledge from diverse sources, as seen in the analysis of multi-client data systems. In such a system, each client possesses information about the joint distribution of their local data and a global feature, which the proposed federated learning scheme utilizes to incorporate client-specific priors into a common probability distribution. As an extension, the DGD was used to visualize the variability in the combined data and identify distinct characteristics among the individual clients. In situations where the training data is insufficient, the DGD is used as a bootstrapping technique to reinstate a probability distribution, based on earlier training samples. In practical tests, the DGD demonstrates its ability to accurately capture a reversed mapping in the presence of limited data. In contrast to conventional methods, the DGD does not suffer from data inconsistencies when applied to multi-modal data sets. In a series of experiments, the DGD shows its ability to consistently identify the optimal inverse mapping from observations to modalities, based solely on observed data. In conclusion, the DGD analysis contributes to an enhanced understanding of deep generative models and inverse mappings. A publicly accessible code for the DGD is available at: https://github.com/sagar2019/Inverse-Gaussian-Mixtures. Publicly accessible code can also be found at https://github.com/ashishsharma63/Deep-Generative-Decoder. A pre-registered discussion paper can also be found at: https://osf.io/r4ybc/. Recent breakthroughs in neural audio synthesis using unsupervised techniques are
promising to streamline the process of creating high-quality spoken audio from text.
However, it remains unclear whether these unsupervised systems can produce speech of
a similar standard to their supervised counterparts. In this research, we develop an
unsupervised speech synthesis method that generates speech with notably reduced
artifacts and improved coherence, and we demonstrate its capabilities on a large
dataset of raw online text and audio. Our results indicate that this approach can
produce speech that is easily understood and sounds natural, and we conduct a
formal user study which reveals that most listeners cannot distinguish the speech
produced by our unsupervised system from that generated by a supervised system. 

This research is significant because it successfully applies neural audio synthesis to
real-world, uncurated text and audio data, and we speculate that this could have
a significant impact on natural language processing research. Moreover, we envision
that this technology could be used to create spoken language dialects that are
currently disappearing due to the dominance of written language. 

Additionally, we develop an innovative, self-supervised technique for creating
speech synthesis training data by leveraging the relationship between similar text
segments within long sentences. This method allows us to expand a training dataset
of hundreds of hours in just a few hours of computational processing time. 

Ultimately, we believe this research has significant implications for the
distributed, collaborative development of neural audio synthesis models, and we
hope that this research inspires new methods for enhancing these systems. In the
future, we also intend to apply these techniques to other application areas such as
English language training and speech translation. In order to facilitate further
research in this area, we publicly release both our unsupervised speech synthesis
model and the entire research code on GitHub at the address https://github.com/mulesong/unsupSWS.

In summary, this paper contributes a pioneering unsupervised speech synthesis method
that produces high-quality speech with minimal artifacts and improved coherence and
is capable of producing speech synthesis training data from large datasets of uncurated
text and audio. It demonstrates the ability to produce speech that is easily understood
and sounds natural in a relatively short amount of computational processing time and
is able to enhance a supervised model's results in a self-supervised manner. In addition,
it publicly releases a research code base that can be used in other application areas
such as the creation of spoken language dialects, the enhancement of endangered languages

Recent advancements in Supervised Pre-training of Language Models have highlighted its potential in capturing detailed semantic information and achieving improved performance in downstream tasks. However, most of these studies primarily focused on English models, which might not effectively handle Chinese data due to differences in token characteristics and the complexity of Chinese language. In an effort to bridge this gap, we developed a Supervised Contrastive Pre-training model specifically designed for Chinese product reviews, an area that lacks sufficient research. Our proposed model leverages a novel contrastive learning technique that incorporates both token and sentence-level contrastive learning to enhance the model's capture of sentiment-oriented information. Moreover, we designed a sentiment-aware mask objective function to guide the model's learning towards more meaningful sentiment representations. Our extensive experiments involving multiple datasets demonstrate that our proposed model significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art Chinese models in sentiment analysis tasks. These results show that our Supervised Contrastive Pre-training model achieves a remarkable 9.5% absolute improvement in F1-score compared to the strongest competitor. Our model's exceptional performance also extends to more challenging sentiment analysis tasks, where it achieves a 6.3% absolute improvement in F1-score when using a more sophisticated evaluation metric. These results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed Supervised Contrastive Pre-training model in achieving improved sentiment analysis performance. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available for download.

This research investigates a reliable MIMO-based RIS-assisted UC MCS system in a reliable environment that takes into account the effects of RIS hardware impairments and jamming from the CIR. A non-linear optimization problem is initially identified to ensure simultaneous maximum data rates for all users in the presence of hardware impairments and jamming. This complex problem is redefined as a non-linear optimization problem with fewer constraints to make it computationally soluble. A novel two-stage algorithm is proposed to find an accurate solution to this problem: In the first stage, the optimal value of $2^{L}-1$ is determined for $m_{opt}$ by iteratively taking into account the effects of hardware impairments. In the second stage, the optimal values of $m_{opt}$ and $p_{opt}$ are obtained by iteratively maximizing a reformulated logarithmic function. The resulting algorithm has a computationally efficient complexity of $\mathcal{O}(2^{5L})$. We present numerical results to validate that our proposed algorithm can achieve optimal results, while also observing that hardware impairments can significantly reduce the optimal power load and resulting interference, thus simplifying the design of reliable UC MCS systems with RIS. For instance, with $K=10$ and $L=5$, increasing the hardware impairments from $0.1$ to $0.8$ results in reducing the optimal power load by $67\%$ and minimizing the resulting interference by $13$ dB. These observations also reveal the significant impact of other parameters such as $b_{min}$, $p_{min}$, $h_{ri}$ and $h_{u}$ on reliable UC MCS systems with RIS. Furthermore, with mass production of RIS-based hardware, the effects of hardware impairments can be minimized, thus making the initial design phase of reliable UC MCS with RIS more accessible. The proposed algorithm has been implemented using the Optizly toolbox and is available at the cited website.

To further investigate, we examined kinetic energy flux density spectra from the MESSENGER spacecraft and compared them to an unknown source near the sun. Assuming an unknown source type, we applied power law and triangular distributions to observe the Helios spacecraft's energy distribution properties. We also used triangular distributions to predict the energy properties of the energy source near the sun. We then compared our results to an earlier study that used triangular distributions to analyze data from the Parker spiral at 1 AU. We discovered that our findings align with an increase in high-energy particles near the sun, in line with helioseismic frequency predictions. We also found that our triangular distribution model accurately fits Energy Spectrum Measurement System observations at both 1 AU and in the Mars Express spacecraft. However, our model's triangular distribution does not accurately represent the MEX's energy distribution. Achieving a direct visual proof of the timelike Unruh effect is challenging due to its elusive nature. An alternative method to detect this phenomenon is proposed, which involves harnessing the power of time-varying $\hbar$-systems. By building an apparatus that leverages these systems, the Unruh paradox can be resolved, allowing the quantum state to track the time evolution of an Unruh detector's quantum states even in stationary conditions. Consequently, the absence of quantum flags - which signify the creation of a quantum state from the vacuum by the Unruh effect - indicates the presence of the timelike Unruh effect. Given that super-luminal information cannot be obtained, a quantum network is suggested that enables a timely and global verification of quantum connections among Unruh detectors without violating causality. An alternative method for detecting the timelike Unruh effect is thus proposed, which not only confirms quantum consistency but also a consistent quantum mechanics without contradictions. Furthermore, the role of gravity in an accelerated Uehara system is identified, which reveals that the Unruh effect can be interpreted as a pre-thermal effect arising from the pre-thermalization of an initial pure quantum state. Ultimately, the timelike Unruh effect is identified as an emergent macroscopic quantum phenomenon arising from the pre-thermalization of an initial pure quantum state, which is an inherent property of any quantum system coupled to a thermal bath - even a vacuum. Therefore, the proposed method presents a potential new way to identify the timelike Unruh effect using an apparatus based on $\hbar$-systems coupled to a time-dependent quantum harmonic oscillator representing the Uehara's quantum network. As an added benefit, the power of quantum computing can be leveraged to analyze complex time-dependent $\hbar$-systems, thus accelerating experimental verification of the proposed method. Moreover, an alternative method for identifying quantum information without breaching causality can be proposed, which involves exploiting the interconnections among Unruh detectors. Ultimately, the Unruh paradox can be resolved not only by identifying the timelike effect but also by confirming the consistent application of quantum mechanics without contradictions, which leads to a new understanding of the pre-thermal effect arising from the pre-thermalization of an initial pure quantum state as an emergent macroscopic quantum phenomenon. Furthermore, potential applications can be suggested, which involves exploiting the unique characteristics of the pre-thermal effect to design a quantum network without violating causality, which may pave the way for developing novel technologies based on a consistent quantum mechanics

This research tackles the problem of extracting complex event information from text, an operation normally performed by sophisticated NLP systems but proves notoriously difficult for human translators when applied to Japanese texts. Despite recent advancements in NLP technology for translating Japanese text into English, we investigated whether machines built for English can effectively analyze Japanese events. Our research reveals that these systems struggle greatly with Japanese data, likely due to the unique characteristics of the Japanese language. In response, we developed a state-of-the-art single system capable of accurately extracting and organizing complex events, achieving a remarkable 71.3% overall extraction precision. Our system utilizes a BERT model combined with a multi-stage, multi-output approach that capitalizes on the language model's inherent abilities. Additionally, we adapted the multi-stage framework to incorporate previous knowledge from English into the Japanese domain, showcasing improved extraction performance. Our thorough evaluation through comprehensive testing and analysis confirms that the extracted information surpasses that of human performance in a related task, an accomplishment considered highly challenging due to the differences between the two languages. The proposed method and associated resources are available for public use and could help expand the use of sophisticated NLP technology for analyzing Japanese events. Furthermore, the multi-stage framework could provide valuable insights for developing more efficient and accurate NLP systems across various domains, an operation currently limited to English.
