Automated evaluation of summarization models and human-written summaries remains a pressing issue. Current diversity metrics are inadequate, and existing automatic evaluation metrics lack accuracy in relation to human-generated scores. This paper presents SummScore, a novel evaluation metric that rewards precise and diverse summary representations. By incorporating a novel fine-tuning approach for abstractive summarization models, SummScore is designed to optimize performance over a wide range of its predecessor, recently shown to outperform existing metrics in terms of precision and relevance. Experiments conducted on the Google Dataset Search dataset have shown that SummScore is more closely aligned with human-generated scores and outperforms existing diversity metrics. Furthermore, SummScore has successfully improved the performance of the underlying models, making it a superior evaluation metric in the process. The proposed diversity-preserving evaluation framework is made publicly available at the link provided.

In recent years, sparse recovery techniques have gained significant attention. These methods typically rely on data being sparse in a specific domain and employ techniques such as l1-regularization or dictionary learning to recover sparse representations. However, in many practical scenarios, observed data is cross-correlated and therefore, cannot be treated as independent samples. For such scenarios, we present a novel sparse recovery algorithm that relies on a cross-covariance pattern without requiring prior knowledge of this pattern. Notably, our algorithm is capable of recovering sparse representations in both the feature space and the covariance space. A key advantage of this algorithm is its ability to adapt to varying levels of data sparsity and cross-correlation patterns. Furthermore, our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm in recovering relevant cross-covariance patterns, while also showcasing its ability to handle challenging scenarios through simulation studies. These studies show that the amount of sparsity that can be recovered increases with the availability of more cross-correlated data. In order to facilitate the application of this algorithm in a broad range of fields, we have made its implementation available as an open-source package called 'CrossCovarianceDictionaryLearning', which is available at https://github.com/erdong-xu/CrossCovarianceDictionaryLearning. This package provides a user-friendly interface for reproancing the experiments presented in this work and allows researchers to perform additional studies. Furthermore, an accompanying code repository containing the implementation of the CCAL algorithm can also be accessed at https://github.com/erdong-xu/CCALCodeRepository. This research delves into object detection within urban environments using the combination of city sensor information and 3D object detection technology. Existing approaches typically concentrate on utilizing a single urban sensor source, such as cameras or LiDAR, despite being imperfect and leading to a lack of consistency in object detection. City sensors, including cameras and LiDAR, sometimes neglect to identify objects due to factors like obstruction or failure. Conversely, a novel BEVFusion framework is proposed, designed to fuse data from multiple urban sensors simultaneously. By designing a dual object detection system, the incorporation of sensor failures is automatically accommodated within the model. A training dataset, comprising around 70,000 3D object ground truths from the SUN RGB-D dataset, the KITTI dataset, and the NuScenes dataset, is utilized to facilitate learning. A comprehensive evaluation, comprising an extensive dataset derived from a combination of the Waymo Open Dataset, the CarPKLOT dataset, and the NuScenes dataset, demonstrates that the proposed BEVFusion model outperforms current standards by a significant margin, including a 2.3% and 1.5% improvement in missing hard easy IoU in the presence of LiDAR and camera failures respectively. Moreover, the proposed approach exceeds current standards by 11.3% and 14.1% for hard easy missing easy in the presence of LiDAR and camera failures respectively. The explosive growth in IoT devices has led to an overwhelming quantity of event stream data that need to be processed instantly. Current stream processing languages and operators are unable to cope with such data due to velocity and volumacity challenges. In response, we introduce H-STREAM, a novel streaming data model tailored to manage high-speed and high-volume streams from IoT devices. H-STREAM considers the inherent time constraints and device specifications of IoT data sources. It encompasses a comprehensive set of streaming algebraic operators that can be executed concurrently in a fully parallel manner. We also developed an efficient execution layer for H-STREAM, resulting in significant performance improvements in comparative experiments against leading stream processing frameworks. The framework and sources behind H-STREAM are freely available online at the address: https://sites.google.com/view/hstream-framework/.

This paper proposes a novel model that builds upon the strengths of existing models by incorporating a copy mechanism to improve its performance in the SPARQL domain. The model can effectively leverage information from question features and copy data from a knowledge base without a prior lexical match. Through comprehensive experiments using the QASparql dataset, we demonstrate the benefits of the new model in terms of accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. Notably, the results show that the proposed model achieves a significant 11.1% improvement in exact match accuracy over state-of-the-art models. Further analysis of the model's performance reveals its capacity for robustness, with 72.7% of all exact exact matches generated through the copy mechanism. Additionally, the model's interpretability is demonstrated through the identification of specific patterns in copiable questions and their corresponding copiable phrases. This insight has the potential to enhance the design of more efficient query generation models in the future. Furthermore, by using the proposed model to enhance question features, we discover several intriguing patterns that can further improve existing models. For instance, questions containing the copiable phrase "the capital of" consistently rank top in terms of exact match accuracy. Moreover, the model training data highlights a notable data imbalance between questions with and without lexical matches, as 85.5% of all exact exact matches occur in questions that contain lexical matches. These findings are highly informative and can be utilized to design more efficient query generation models in the future. Overall, the proposed model represents a substantial advancement in the SPARQL query generation domain in terms of both accuracy and robustness. While there is still a significant gap between human and machine performance, the insights gained from this research have the potential to inform the development of more efficient and accurate query generation models in the future. Consequently, the proposed model's source code, along with other supplementary materials, is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/mori-uchicago/SPARQL-CG. This enables fellow researchers to build upon our findings and develop the next-generation SPARQL query generation models. Furthermore, based on our model's recommendations, we discover several areas for enhancing future data enrichment efforts in the DBpedia dataset. A customized tool has been designed to gather and organize the vast amount of data from numerous publishing venues and their archives. Furthermore, a interactive visualization platform displaying publishing venue data is available on our research group's website. A key challenge is ensuring the design produces controllers that can withstand unforeseen sensor data disruptions. In this paper, we highlight progress made in verifying robustness using techniques from computer vision and machine learning, which offer powerful tools for analyzing controller behavior under various sensor data scenarios. Additionally, we present a framework for combining computer vision and reinforcement learning methodologies to design robust neural network controllers. Evaluating these methods using a specific application - autonomous flight - demonstrates the potential for significant, safe performance enhancements when using robust neural network controllers derived from our approach. In contrast to existing methods, our framework does not require a comprehensive, detailed model of the system to be controlled. This research marks a first step in integrating recent advancements in vision and learning to enhance control system design. With ongoing developments in deep learning, the implications of these methods for neural network control systems, and the safety of their applications will continue to evolve. We aim to provide early insights into this emerging research area before safety concerns potentially undermine its promise. The study also highlights crucial challenges, points of integration, and potential research pathways where natural language processing can contribute to neural network control systems for their safety critical applications. Furthermore, it offers guidance on tackling system-level challenges rather than merely leveraging pre-existing models, and encourages the utilization of learning methods capable of generalization. In the future, the integration of vision, learning, and verification is likely to substantially enhance the reliability and hence, the safety of neural network control systems. In particular, it will enable the development of learning and control strategies where exposure to failure at operational conditions may not necessarily lead to large-scale accidents. For instance, it will ensure that successful learned controllers achieve through a systematic design process, avoid adverse system responses across a wide array of possible disruptions, and minimize accidents. Ultimately, it will pave the way towards achieving a systematic and systematic design of learning and control strategies that are informed by the principles of cybernetics and engineering, which will significantly lower the risk of unintended harm to people and the environment. In addition, it will offer an unparalleled ability to predict and mitigate the likelihood of failure during operational runtime by analyzing and measuring the relationship between learned parameters and robustness. By examining the linkage graph of this relation, where clusters are merged based on a nearest approach, we reveal a critical issue that affects its cluster quality. We subsequently develop two functorial clustering schemes that address this problem and provide new insights into single-linkage clustering. In addition, we define a type of 'exotic' cluster called an S-cluster, which is formed using the equivalence relation $S_0$. We show that the traditional single-linkage clusters are a subset of S-clusters, and establish a stochastic process that converges to S-clusters. This process has a higher cluster quality compared to single-linkage clustering and does not require correction terms at large sample sizes. Moreover, we introduce a novel type of hierarchical tree, known as the S-tree, which represents the hierarchical structure of S-clusters. We prove that the median hierarchical tree of single-linkage clusters is a special case of the S-tree and establish that the S-tree has multiple desirable properties. To illustrate the performance of our approach, we compare the cluster quality of S-clusters with that of single-linkage clusters using real and simulated data. The results demonstrate that, on average, S-clusters have improved cluster quality and are within a constant factor of single-linkage clusters. We further develop a data analysis tool to automatically determine optimal sample size for reliable clustering using the equivalence relation $S_0$. In particular, we show that $S_0$ offers different merging conditions for points in a metric space, which enables the application of Theorem 1.1 of Aldous and Shields to find the minimal required sample size. The tool is utilized in our analysis of clustering issues in quantum particle approaches. The increasing use of streaming videos in various fields has led to a growing need for accurate and timely knowledge graphs. A key step in creating and maintaining these graphs is streaming tensor completion, which aims to forecast missing data in streaming tensor videos based on the observed data. Existing streaming tensor completion algorithms often overlook the motion between video frames, which can provide crucial data for prediction. In this study, a new approach called motion-aware streaming tensor completion (MoST) is presented that captures the correlation between video frames and incorporates contextual information. A tensor completion model is combined with a neural motion predictor to estimate the missing data, and an optimization method is developed to jointly train the model and improve performance. Experimental results demonstrate that MoST significantly outperforms existing streaming tensor completion algorithms, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency. By applying this method, a higher accuracy can be achieved for forecasting missing data in streaming tensor videos. Code for this purpose can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/MOSSONG/MoST. Commercial-scale verification of the proposed method can be seen in a video sharing platform, U-View, developed by Huawei, which supports streaming tensor knowledge graph construction and streaming tensor completion. As shown in the platform, the proposed method and its underlying technologies can achieve excellent performance and run efficiently on common devices. Moreover, the platform allows users to provide third-party models for streaming tensor completion through an open API, making it possible for researchers to contribute their own algorithms and implement them on the platform. A call for participation can be found at https://uview-dev.github.io/call_for_research/. As the use of streaming videos continues to grow, the research community is encouraged to contribute their expertise and help develop accurate and timely knowledge graphs. Furthermore, the underlying technology of the proposed method can be extended to other applications, such as object detection, image recognition, video analytics, intelligent driving, medical imaging, and robotic systems, which rely heavily on tensor completion and motion prediction. Lastly, the oscillator operators are shown to be isospectral with their conjugate counterparts. Importantly, the results obtained, though derived from operator theory in free space, are also applicable in media with point-like interactions. Finally, the results obtained are compared with well-known examples. This paper presents a temporal knowledge graph model that incorporates temporal aspects through a grid-based attention mechanism. This approach treats time progression as a grid, where each point represents a state of temporal progression, and models its relationship with date embeddings as transitions between these states. This method allows for the exploration of temporal evolution in greater detail, particularly when dealing with cyclic patterns. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed model surpasses existing baseline models in multiple metrics. Furthermore, an ablation study reveals that the integration of temporal grid attention significantly enhances representation quality, and that the model's ability to capture consistent temporal trends and structure on grids is a valuable feature for accurate knowledge graph representation. This method is now available as the TensorALibrary on GitHub at the address: https://github.com/leverone/TensorALibrary. All the experiments were conducted using the TKG DataHub platform at the address: datahub.io. Finally, a detailed analysis of parameters and training loss curves provides valuable insights into the model's performance during training. In the context of asynchronous online federated learning, we have found that a communication strategy based on partial sharing and tailored to individual users, can yield better outcomes compared to the central server's optimized model. By allowing clients to locally optimize towards different objectives, and then sharing only the necessary information with each other and the server, partial sharing facilitates more efficient communication. We introduce a new partial sharing mechanism which combines compression and quantization techniques based on gradient phase change, resulting in significant reduction of communication latency. This approach optimizes information transmission from clients and the server, while keeping the accuracy of the global model at a minimum cost. We experimentally validated our proposed method in scenarios involving non-collaborating and non-optimal federated learning settings, observing a 77.3% reduction in server-latency and a 61.3% reduction in client-latency, without a corresponding loss in accuracy. These empirical findings indicate that a communication strategy based on partial sharing and tailored to individual users, can lead to a 24.4% and 35.6% increase in latency for non-collaborative and non-optimal federated learning settings, respectively. Ultimately, our proposed method has shown potential to enhance the efficiency of asynchronous online federated learning systems. As these systems are susceptible to accuracy losses due to compression, we suggest employing techniques such as noise-cancellation, interleaving, and de-noising that prioritize compression-quality over compression-ratio, resulting in improved performance. We have observed a significant boost in the precision of the global model, resulting in a maximum 99.1% and an average 91.6%, in scenarios involving partial sharing and compression, without a corresponding loss. We recommend exploring the potential synergy between the proposed partial sharing mechanism and compression techniques in order to further optimize the accuracy of the global model and elevate the efficiency of asynchronous online federated learning settings. A combined theoretical and experimental study focuses on silicon films, micrometer-sized plates, and nanoparticles, against the background of silicon oxide. Electrostatic forces can confine electrons in various geometries - energy can be supplied to these systems through an external stimulus, either mechanical or optical, which can also be used for heating purposes by providing incident light. We derive these functions by solving certain integral equations, which can be interpreted as a complex version of the Airy function, evaluated at specific points. We further provide a physical interpretation by linking these functions to the dynamics of the exponential map. One potential candidate, FR-12, has passed initial pharmacological and toxicology assessments and is now being further evaluated in clinical studies to determine its efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in adults. Since humans absorb nicotine primarily in the stomach, research into its use in humans is expediated by in vitro testing with donor stomachs. A difficulty in nicotine research arises from the physical phase transition, which affects the rate of nicotine release. To address this, an experimental setup with two interconnected chambers was designed to optimize the vapor density and minimize temperature variations between the inner and outer environments. Observations were made over a 30-minute period using an infrared camera, which measured temperatures and inferred vapor densities. The architecture and procedures were then refined for use in larger-scale human clinical trials, providing insights into nicotine absorption in the stomach through imaging and chemical analysis. This framework examines a specific type of optical signal, known as a polarization-multiplexed code division multiple access signal, within a fiber network that includes multiple components such as light sources, devices that randomize and weaken the signal, and devices that filter the signal. By analyzing how the signal is affected by components that randomly change the signal, researchers use the model to make predictions about the performance of the system. Building on prior research, the model is validated by comparing its predictions to experimental results. Consistent with these predictions, the model shows how errors in the signal, known as bit errors, are influenced by various system parameters both individually and interactively. By mathematically optimizing these system parameters, the model reveals the optimal configuration, which aligns with experimental findings and enhances the experimental maximum performance capacity. Additionally, the model predicts an optimal level of signal weakening that corresponds with experimental results. By incorporating these predictions into a statistical model, the total probability distribution of signal weakening is described. Also, the model gives a detailed statistical description of how errors are distributed along the devices that weaken the signal. Multi-spectral and infrared images have different sensitivity ranges, capturing images in multiple spectral ranges can reveal more details than a single image in visible light. This notion led to the development of image fusion, enabling the creation of an all-around view with fewer limitations. Narrow filters in narrow band images and high sensitivity in multi-spectral images result in poor visual quality and limited useful data, making narrow band images dominant in visible, multi-spectral, and thermal band images less effective. This research presents an analysis of fire images combined using a deep learning technique, assessing its performance in an automated fire detection system. By comparing traditional and deep learning-based image fusion methods, we evaluate their efficacy and reliability in a fire detection context. We also examine the potential of employing more than one thermal band for enhanced fire detection capabilities. Our findings indicate that fire imagery can be effectively combined using deep learning-based techniques, resulting in a lower false positive rate in comparison to narrow band images. This, in turn, creates opportunities for the development of automated fire detection systems utilizing image fusion. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that incorporating multiple thermal bands does not always yield improved results, suggesting that certain fire objects may not consistently generate sufficient thermal signals. We also propose the potential for deep learning-based image fusion to be applied in automated fire detection systems, examining its practicality and effectiveness in such systems. By visually analyzing the images combined using different methods, we verified that fire imagery can be effectively combined and that high-quality combined images may reduce false positives. We also hypothesize that incorporating bias in the image fusion process could be used to create homogenous combined images, leading to the development of automated fire detection systems that utilize combined images with an inherent bias. By comparing the effectiveness of different image fusion methods on niche detection tasks such as fire detection, we highlight the potential for further research in this area and identify areas for improvement. We also compare the performance of different image fusion methods, demonstrating that while bias may result in inferior combined images, it can make combined images with less variability more effective in detecting fires. Notably, our analysis shows that bias may result in negative outcomes in certain situations, such as when the bias creates hotspots that may mislead detectors. We also reveal that incorporating bias in image fusion can result in decreased performance, both generally and in the context of the fire dataset we created. By examining the behavior of different image fusion methods, we gain insights into their mechanics and potential applications, both in the context of fire detection and in other niche detection tasks. Diagnosing mental health conditions through social media analysis has gained significant attention in recent research. Initially met with skepticism due to its unorthodox nature, this method has proven effective, albeit requiring further investigation. Consequently, we conducted a comprehensive review of the current state of mental health detection systems that utilize social media. The primary goal of this examination is to establish whether social media data can be relied upon to diagnose mental health, compared to traditional diagnostic methods that rely on clinical evaluations. The comparison involves considering the advantages and limitations of social media-based systems in terms of their accuracy, diversity, and the scope of applicable algorithms. Furthermore, we discussed the challenges associated with utilizing social media data for mental health analysis, as well as potential future research directions and applications. The discussion centers around the hypothesis that social media data can be an efficient substitute, rather than a supplement, to traditional clinical evaluations. The outcome of this exploration may lead to the development of advanced systems that utilize social media data to provide insights into mental health, revolutionizing the diagnosis process. The review of relevant literature may also reveal areas for further research, facilitating the creation of a functional mental health diagnosis system based on social media data. The evaluation criteria used in this examination include precision, diversity, complexity, and the variety of algorithms employed, with specific weights assigned to each criterion. The evaluation process involved analyzing 43 studies spanning a period of 11 years, with the majority employing data mining-based algorithms. The Diabetic Retention Rate and ROC Area were used as primary and secondary evaluation metrics, respectively. The social hermeneutic circle, consisting of three stages including interpretation, analysis, and context, was employed as the theoretical framework for this examination. The application of social media-based systems for mental health analysis is increasingly significant due to their scale, diversity, and the scope they cover. The manuals, guidelines, and technical specifications provided by institutions regarding social media data analysis for mental health analysis enhance its validity, reliability, and applicability. The use of social media-based systems for mental health analysis may lead to the development of diagnosis systems that are efficient, effective, and economical, paving the way for widespread adoption. The objective of intuitive recommendation systems lies in comprehending users' underlying intentions. Although several sequenced models have been applied to extract user goals from interactive histories, their open-domain operation causes them to be sidetracked by unimportant details in the history sequence. This paper proposes a user intent model specifically designed for goal extraction, focused solely on user intent and optimized for both small and large datasets. In this context, PCA involves operating on a weighted sum of data sets. Our in-depth analysis reveals that PCA achieves an optimal decomposition when data sets share the same principal components and scale. Consequently, PCA excels in situations where either numerous or highly correlated datasets are involved. However, when the possibility of shared principal components is minimal and weighted combinations are random, more sophisticated techniques like nuclear norm minimization (NNM) and maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) surpass PCA in terms of baseline performance. Additionally, we introduce and closely analyze several other approximation methods as competing baselines in this context. The primary objective of this research is to examine the interplay between environmental changes and the adaptations that result from them at multiple levels of biological organization, focusing specifically on the interplay between ecological and evolutionary processes. To achieve this goal, we investigate how variations in temperature and mutation rate influence the dynamics of continuous adaptations, exploring their effects on the rate of change, the diversity of adaptations, and the likelihood of mutualistic interactions between different species. Through a combination of theoretical modeling and simulation-based analyses, we uncover a complex interplay between these processes and the role of temperature and mutation rate in shaping their outcomes. Notably, our findings suggest that higher mutation rates tend to stabilize ecological interactions, while temperature fluctuations have a more profound and far-reaching impact on both ecological and evolutionary processes. Moreover, our results indicate that temperature-related variations can lead to shifts from mutualism to competition, and that both ecological and evolutionary processes can exhibit similar patterns of behavior in response to temperature changes. Ultimately, our research highlights the crucial need for models that integrate multiple scales of biological organization to better grasp the complex consequences of environmental changes on adaptive processes. Using a dataset comprising proton-proton collisions at a 7 TeV centre-of-mass energy, collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to 1 fb-1 of integrated luminosity, the fragmentation of heavy quarks is studied. The data are particularly examined to analyse the fragmentation of charm and beauty quarks, where it is observed that strange mesons play a crucial role. The analysis focuses on two variables: the fraction of heavy quarks carried by the meson and the momentum distribution of the meson itself. The results reveal that fragmentation fractions involving the strange meson Lambda are notably higher for beauty quarks compared to charm quarks, by about 0.2 standard deviations. This discrepancy could hint at a potential bias related to the momentum of heavy quarks, where it is observed that strange mesons are more frequently produced at higher momenta due to the decay of b-hadrons. The results are discussed in comparison to theoretical models from PEPPARC and pQPM. The analysis highlights the difficulty in comparing data to models due to the extensive uncertainty in input parameters, especially for beauty quarks, and the need for further comparison with different fragmentation functions. The LHCb experiment is uniquely positioned to study heavy quark fragmentation, thanks to its preservation of the full event shape information throughout hadronisation. The analysis paves the way for potential applications in particle identification, particularly for rare b-hadron decays, where it is observed that strange mesons play a crucial role in detection. The validity of several mass and momentum conservation models is tested using data on the momentum distribution of the strange meson Lambda. The results confirm the validity of the PEPPARC model for both charm and beauty quarks, while they are found to be in disagreement with the pQPM model, particularly for beauty quarks. The analysis highlights the extensive uncertainty in the parameter alpha_MN, affecting both data and model predictions, and the need for further comparison with different fragmentation functions. The results will contribute to improving the PEPPARC mass calibration for both charm and beauty quarks, by reducing uncertainty in the parameter alpha_MN by about 20%. The LHCb experiment is poised to expand its understanding of the strange meson Lambda by studying its production in b-hadron decays, thus advancing the field of strange meson Lambda particle identification. The problem of shifting matrix inverse estimation involves determining the most effective way to shift a noisy matrix, A, towards a target matrix, B. This shift can be achieved by optimizing either the shift vector, t, or the matrix C, which contains the shift vector as one of its elements. Our study focuses on finding an optimal shift that minimizes a sparse regularization term, and we identify two fundamental versions of this problem. One version assumes noise asymmetry and finds that the optimal shift direction is always aligned with the difference between individual matrix entries. Conversely, the other version assumes noise symmetry and reveals that there are multiple optimal shifts, which are equally good and lie on an elliptical shape. Our results demonstrate that these findings hold regardless of the specific sparsity level. Furthermore, our numerical experiments confirm that incorporating knowledge about noise symmetry significantly enhances matrix estimation quality compared to the case where assumptions are not applied. Additionally, our results show that optimizing either the shift vector or the shift matrix according to our new theory yields better results than consistently optimizing either the shift vector or the shift matrix according to symmetry assumptions. Lastly, our study highlights that the optimal shift value increases as sparsity level increases, and provides additional insights into specific problem scenarios. We introduce Landmark Gabor Filters, a novel image representation method, which achieves heightened resistance to variations in orientation and reduced sensitivity to minor reorientations through the strategic placement of landmarks in Gabor filters. This approach ensures that the pattern of local intensity maxima remains consistent even in cases of moderate reorientation. The Landmark Gabor Filters' robustness to orientation can be leveraged to develop efficient, localized image descriptors based on the common Gabor-based image representation. Moreover, LGFs serve as a significant step forward in the family of Gabor filters used for image representation and serve as a novel method for extracting meaningful local features from images. We illustrate the practical utility of our representation method in a local image descriptor called LGBM, which outperforms existing local features and descriptors across a range of benchmark tests, including robustness, accuracy of matching, and resistance to noise. Ultimately, this novel representation method offers enhanced capabilities in both static image understanding, particularly in the context of Gabor-based image representation, and the field of visual odometry. When recommendation systems are questioned, managers often turn to post-hoc analyses in an effort to understand and adapt to changing user behavior. Although these explanations are frequently relied upon, research has not thoroughly investigated their impact on the accuracy of recommendation models. In this research, a double natural experiment is conducted involving a real-world online shopping recommendation system, which provides explicit justification for why specific items were recommended. By examining this system, a comparative analysis is made between models that receive post-hoc explanations and those that do not, using a twin framework to measure variation in model performance in response to changes in user behavior. The results indicate a notable difference in model stability when trained with a dataset that incorporates post-hoc explanations, which were found to exacerbate model vulnerabilities to certain types of data manipulations. Consequently, a more thorough examination of the underlying architecture and a more realistic evaluation of a recommendation system's robustness is advised, encompassing both natural user behavior and adversarial data on multiple modes. Furthermore, researchers and developers should be cautious when utilizing explanations derived from reinforcement learning for action-taking purposes, as these explanations can sometimes suggest infeasible actions that would be preferred by reinforcement learning algorithms optimizing action-taking over explanation-generating. The issue of class overfitting after an excessive increase in the majority class size through simple data augmentation has long been a concern, prompting the development of more sophisticated methods to address this problem. In response, a novel method utilizing hybrid adversarial learning for creating balanced data distributions is presented. This approach combines the capabilities of a generated major class classifier and an adaptive discriminator, which helps the minor class learner avoid poor predictions by creating a signal for the minor class boundary for the minor class learner. This method demonstrates the ability to significantly improve the minor class accuracy and derive a more reliable minor class model. Two real-world data sets, which are known to be heavily skewed towards the minority class, were used in an experiment. Our research found that the hybrid adversarial approach not only boosts minority class accuracy, but also achieves a more significant increase in the overall balanced Accuracy measure compared to simple data augmentation. Furthermore, an experiment involving a synthetic data set revealed that the simple data augmentation method falls prey to a bias towards overfitting, resulting in a lack of generalizability. On the other hand, a hybrid adversarial approach was shown to be resistant to overfitting and therefore capable of providing better predictions on unseen data. In conclusion, the proposed method differs significantly from traditional overfitting prevention methods, as it seeks to address the issue of class overfitting through a balanced data distribution rather than simple data augmentation. At the heart of this technique lies a unique hybrid adversarial approach that prevents the creation of a biased model. This research contributes towards a better understanding of how data and model interactions influence class overfitting and provide insights into developing improved algorithms for creating a more balanced data distribution in the future. By manipulating the dot's electrical charge via tunnel junctions, researchers can create a range of different superconductor-dot-superconductor configurations, allowing for the study of how quasiparticles transition across the dot at temperatures below the critical temperature of the superconductor. This setup can then be used to investigate the fermion exchange current between the two superconductors and the dot, giving insight into how a ferromagnetic impurity affects the addition spectrum of a connected superconductor. Moreover, by utilizing two tunnel junctions rather than one, researchers can directly measure this exchange current and its impact on the two superconductors. Finally, our set-up can also be used to study a broader range of quantum phenomena, such as the long-range Andreev interaction, the backscattering of low-energy quasiparticles, and the dot's ferromagnetic properties. All of these properties can be controlled through external gate voltages, allowing for a range of different conditions to be studied. Perpetual view generation is the task of creating an infinite number of viewpoints for a given object, a challenge that has been ongoing for over three decades. Our research redefines this task by focusing on developing an unsupervised method to produce dynamic, multi-person perspective view generation. We achieve this by leveraging two key networks: one that identifies and matches recurring patterns across moving individuals, and another that combines these matches to produce viewpoints from unseen angles. We also introduce a set of rules to ensure that the generated views are logical and consistent with the underlying structure of the scene. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses previous approaches in both qualitative and quantitative assessments. Additionally, we introduce the Deep Perpetual Synthetic Training dataset to enable the training of our model without human annotation. We also introduce the Perpetual View Generation dataset to evaluate our model's performance. The approach first modifies complex geometries by converting them into Lagrangian coordinates, where the metric is unique. It then applies the Clebsch representation to the Navier-Stokes equations in this new coordinate system. This study assesses the reliability of using a robotic ultrasound to track the curvature of the spine in scoliosis patients. On one side of the spine, the robotic ultrasound successfully measured the angle of the curvature with moderate reliability. However, it did not provide reliable measurements of the length of the spine's curve, especially in patients with shorter curves. When trying to align images from the ultrasound with preoperative 3D images, the process showed poor reliability. While the robotic ultrasound showed some reliability in measuring the depth of spinal curvature, it was inconsistent in doing so. These findings highlight the limitations of using robotic ultrasound for measuring spinal deformities. Further research is needed to improve this technique's effectiveness, especially in combining it with other imaging techniques. This study also suggests that robotic ultrasound could be useful for continuously monitoring spinal curvature during surgical procedures, but more studies are required to confirm this. Generally, the accuracy of robotic ultrasound measurements was within 2 degrees for curvature angles and 5 mm for length measurements. Significant discrepancies were found in the measurement of spinal features like vertebral body shape and posterior height. These inaccuracies may stem from the poor image quality obtained, especially when looking perpendicular to the spine. This study suggests that robotic ultrasound is not yet suitable for estimating spinal curvature. However, it has the potential to monitor real-time movements during surgical procedures or provide estimates of limb length. Images captured by the robotic ultrasound remain clear and concise, enabling real-time analysis. This study is significant in that it is the first to examine the reliability of robotic ultrasound measurements in the spine, providing a foundation for further research on this technology. These findings indicate that the robotic ultrasound needs improvement, specifically in its ability to capture spinal features from the side. Consequently, attempts to use it for aligning 2D and 3D images or serving as an image substitute have proven ineffective. These results highlight several potential avenues to enhance the robotic ultrasound, specifically in improving its ability to capture images in the sagittal plane, increasing its field of view, utilizing artificial intelligence, or merging data with other imaging techniques. These modifications could ultimately yield a highly portable, easy-to-use, and efficient tool for continuously monitoring spinal curvature during surgical procedures. Such a device could also provide real-time feedback to inform real-time preoperative or intraoperative applications. These potential applications will be explored in more depth in future studies. In the near future, the robotic ultrasound is expected to contribute to real-time surgical guidance, provide estimates of spinal curvature, or enable continuous monitoring during procedures. This paper suggests treating duration intensity functions as a special type of neural network transformation that varies over space and time. By doing so, it becomes feasible to model any shape of duration distribution without making any prior assumptions about its form. Moreover, the method enables direct prediction of duration distributions rather than having to choose from a limited set of pre-defined shapes. To accomplish this goal, the paper argues in favor of a simplified strategy for transforming density functions into intensity functions and proposes a neural network that can adapt to these density functions. In addition, the method incorporates a noise term into the network framework, an approach that is analogous to doing the same for outcomes in mean-zero regression models. Finally, the paper presents numerical evidence demonstrating its superior performance on a variety of applications. Specifically, it is shown that when used in survival analysis, the method is capable of generating more accurate predictions for hazard ratios and survival probabilities than conventional models. Furthermore, the paper illustrates the potential applications of this type of neural network by analyzing not only survival data but also time-to-antibody response in the context of HIV trials, as well as P50 values in the context of genomic studies. Interestingly, the method reveals that the distribution of P50 values is notably skewed, exhibiting a significant "tail-and-hump" pattern that can be accurately captured. In addition to these analyses, the method is also demonstrated using actual data from a variety of applications, including an in-depth examination of the distribution of P50 values and the predicted values obtained from the model. While working with this type of neural network presents some unique challenges, the method is surprisingly resilient to inaccuracies in density function specifications that might be expected to cause significant distortions in intensity functions. To illustrate this point, the method is tested using data from a variety of sources, including Google's dataset on US cities. Notably, the method is found to generate predictions that are consistent with Google's data on city-level traffic patterns. Finally, the paper shows that the method is capable of accommodating a wide range of neural network architectures, including some that are significantly larger than others. While working with larger networks is generally expected to cause significant computational difficulties, the method is surprisingly computationally efficient. To illustrate this point, the method is tested using data from a variety of sources, including a challenging simulation study that finds no significant differences in computation times even with very large networks. In conclusion, the paper presents a novel approach to duration modeling that is grounded in a simple neural network framework for transforming density functions into intensity functions. This study aims to compare the efficiency of supervised, unsupervised, weak supervision, active learning and semi-supervised machine learning methods in detecting hate speech. Although extensive research on NLP has produced impressive models, accessible and versatile tools with clear explanations remain a challenge. To address this, we create an actionable HatEval pipeline consisting of text preprocessing, hate speech classification, and generation of clear, executable results applicable to real-life scenarios. Our initial step involves gathering data from relevant sources and developing a comprehensive dataset containing labels, as well as unlabeled texts, including English tweets from the Twitter HateEval dataset and Bulgarian comments from HatEval-BG. Our experiments confirm that active learning, characterized by high human interaction, outperforms other machine learning methods in predicting hate speech in the Bulgarian data set, with a macro F1 score of 0.73, which surpasses the scores of unsupervised (0.43) and weak supervision (0.53) methods. Semi-supervised machine learning also yields better results, with a macro F1 score of 0.73. For comparison, the best macro F1 score in the English dataset is 0.84. Furthermore, active learning (0.73) outperforms semi-supervised (0.69) and weak supervision (0.53) methods, although it slightly lags behind the supervised approach (0.84). Overall, this study contributes an implementable HatEval pipeline, including machine learning code and HatEval-BG dataset, to support NLP researchers in evaluating and comparing different models and labels. Additionally, the HatEval pipeline provides an accessible tool for various stakeholders to identify and mitigate hate speech in the Bulgarian language by taking advantage of the active learning process with a minimal budget of labeled data. With further training on a larger dataset, this pipeline has the potential to expand its applicability to the broader Bulgarian language population. The research also underscores the necessity of a more extensive dataset with high-quality annotations for accurate hate speech detection in the Bulgarian data set. The HatEval pipeline is deployable on cloud platforms such as Google Cloud Platform, Microsoft Azure, and Amazon Web Services. The research, code, dataset, pipeline, as well as executed commands and preprocessed data, can be retrieved from the repository at https://github.com/AlexShagalov/HatEval. A novel method for jointly reconstructing signals, separating complex components, and estimating MIMO subnetworks is established and tested. Our approach requires minimal assumptions, as evidenced by the lack of predefined roles for MIMO subnetworks and the assumption that each subnetwork has a low-rank matrix representation. A key step in this method involves a correntropy-based unmixing process to identify subnetworks, which improves upon previous observations of separate MIMO subnetworks having lower activation rates than solitary networks. By applying the correntropy measure, we can generate a robust loss function that is less affected by noise. A two-stage algorithm is derived from the augmented correntropy based on low-rank structure, which is efficient and can be optimized through alternating optimization. A reliable algorithm is developed for estimating underlying matrices, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments with various synthetic and real-world datasets, including consideration of different noise models and a specific scenario involving brain functional networks and clinical indices for Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, the method reveals insights into subnetworks, such as those associated with distinct genes, and explores their overlap and functional interconnections. A new theoretical framework is proposed, which provides proof of uniqueness and stability for the estimated matrices in a specific regime. According to the results obtained from the tested datasets, the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in joint signal reconstruction and low-rank representation of MIMO subnetworks. A notable advantage of this method is its ability to uncover subnetworks with a resolution that is far greater than previous studies, as evidenced by the number of genes found in functional subnetworks. A link has been established between individual genetic components and specific clinical indices for Alzheimer's disease, which provides valuable quantitative insights for medical professionals. A biological analysis revealed that the subnetworks identified are functionally related to specific biological processes, as evident from GO term analysis. A summary of key findings is provided in the conclusion. The method described here has several benefits and can be adapted for use in module discovery across various fields. A user-friendly R package called CER-MIMO is available for downloading, which provides the necessary implementation details. The package allows researchers to process their own datasets by specifying relevant parameters. CER-MIMO provides detailed documentation and includes all the datasets used for testing, along with precomputed results obtained from the methods described in this paper. A key factor limiting the effectiveness of historical document analysis is locating suitable datasets, due to the limited availability of annotated data online. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces a semi-automated solution to assist researchers in identifying suitable datasets for their specific applications. The proposed method leverages a comprehensive dataset repository with extensive metadata, allowing it to efficiently shortlist relevant datasets based on detailed analysis questions provided by the researchers. By implementing a user interaction framework, this method enables researchers to continuously refine its performance over time, ultimately achieving accurate results in evaluating dataset shortlisting. The benefits of this approach were demonstrated through experiments conducted on a collection of historical document analysis datasets. Additionally, this method provides valuable insights into evaluating different shortlisting hyperparameters, demonstrating its potential to improve interactive machine learning systems for various applications. The accompanying code and dataset repository can be accessed through the following links: https://github.com/AutomaticIndex/dataset-shortling-evaluation and https://github.com/AutomaticIndex/historical-document-analysis-datasets. This research proposes an enhanced approach for achieving precise trajectory tracking in industrial compliant robots. By integrating nonlinear Torque Filter control with adaptive Criss-Cross Dithering (CCD) feedback, our methodology demonstrates superior performance. The key innovation lies in the proposed CCD, which exhibits asymptotic stability and enables robots to accurately follow complex trajectories, particularly around equilibrium points. Current trajectory tracking methods for compliant robots are constrained by their limitations in following smooth curves, necessitating costly pre-calculations, and unsuitable trajectories. To overcome these constraints, our study focuses on enhancing precision for compliant robots, allowing these devices to accurately follow demanding paths, previously inaccessible due to movement constraints. The proposed CCD allows high-accuracy trajectory tracking up to $5\%$, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques. The efficacy of the proposed approach is verified through simulation and experimental validation. The successful implementation of CCD is attributed to its simplicity, compatibility, and adaptability across various applications and existing control frameworks, making it a versatile solution. Furthermore, our methodology estimates the parameters of compliant arms using a novel back-propagation algorithm compatible with non-differentiable optimization methods, enabling accurate modeling and simulation of complex trajectories. To facilitate widespread adoption, our contribution includes open-source implementations of the proposed approach, executable from a command line interface. The simulation results reveal that the trajectories calculated using the proposed method closely resemble the actual movements of the robots, with an accuracy enhancement of up to $3.5\%$. The application of the estimated models allows for the precise simulation of critical scenarios, such as system idleness, with estimated costs of around $0.01-0.03$ seconds. The accuracy of the models also paves the way for the development of automated decision-making tools, including those based on deep learning, which can accurately predict optimal execution times, consistently within $0.02$ seconds. The extensive evaluation of the parameter estimation approach across $120$ trials yields a success rate of nearly $99\%$, with an accuracy enhancement of over $50\%$ compared to current standards. By open-sourcing our code, we aim to accelerate the progress towards the widespread adoption of deep learning-based modeling and simulation for industrial compliant robots. The code is available at https://github.com/robot-learning-group/deep-compliance. Furthermore, our abstract will be presented at the $2022$ Conference. Based on prior research, this paper revisits the study initially published at the $2020$ Conference and incorporates knowledge gained from the international community. This research investigates how socio-demographic factors, such as sex and ethnicity, influence the occurrence of multiple chronic health conditions among myocardial infarction survivors. We develop a multi-condition, multi-timeframe framework to examine the relationship between these factors and the development of various health conditions. By applying a method to identify key factors (Lasso), we create a network that illustrates the interplay between different health conditions over an individual's lifetime. Our findings suggest that survivors of myocardial infarctions commonly experience a combination of conditions such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and stroke. Our model reveals significant disparities in how different ethnic and sexual groups develop these conditions, with some groups, such as the sexual minority group, being more prone to multiple conditions simultaneously. By analyzing the possible connections between different health conditions, we found that there is a high probability of an individual developing multiple conditions if they have already been diagnosed with another condition in the past. In contrast, the relationship between the order in which conditions are diagnosed and co-occurrence is less clear. The statistical significance of the connections between different health conditions was confirmed through cross-validation. A critical component in these models is the modified Becke scheme, which computes integrals involving the electronic continuum, along with derivatives of continuum and solid states. By utilizing an auxiliary basis of Gaussian functions, this scheme enables the efficient computation of these integrals, along with their derivatives. Upon its initial introduction, this method was found to be capable of achieving high precision when applied to a range of wave functions. Nevertheless, its suitability for wave functions that decay slowly, such as those found in Fock-type states, remains uncertain. In an effort to resolve this issue, we have developed an alternative approach to the modified Becke scheme, which replaces Gaussian functions with Bessel functions centered at the boundary of the charge distribution. Investigating the Metric Dimension problem in graphs and networks involves determining the minimum number of probes required to identify any vertex based on the properties of these probes and their distance to other vertices.  This study examines the difficulty of solving the Metric Dimension problem as a function of specific network characteristics such as the number of vertices, clustering number, and the number of connected components in networks.  Our research demonstrates that the problem is particularly challenging if we consider parameters such as vertex number or the clustering number of certain types of graphs, and we highlight a related property of connected graph spaces.  On the other hand, we show that the problem can be efficiently solved in a fixed parameterised setting for specific network structures, and we also develop linear-time algorithms to solve the Metric Dimension problem for specific network types based on the number of vertices.  Finally, we provide a lower bound on the performance of any solution algorithm used to solve the Metric Dimension problem and prove that the problem cannot be efficiently solved by reducing it to a well-known problem that can be efficiently solved.  All our algorithmic results correspond to fixed parameterised settings, and we complement our study with some open questions about the Metric Dimension problem. It is observed that for dcpos in Scott topology, their "convex powerspaces" tend to have upper, lower, and convex variants that are essentially equivalent. However, this equality doesn't hold for Dcpo's "convex powerspace" with Scott topology but it holds for quasi-unifrom Dcpo's "convex powerspace". The concept of convex spaces leads to the introduction of a new topology on Dcpo's that relate uniformly to a set of Dcpo's that are convex. Moreover, it was discovered that the class of Dcpo's that are convex and the class of Dcpo's that are bounded below have disjoint categories when it comes to their Scott topology and the convex spaces' topology. This paper introduces a new approach, BLRM, that utilizes Bayesian statistics to identify and correct mislabeled data in training datasets for deep neural networks, thereby enhancing robustness in data that is contaminated by noise. BLRM relies on a neural network to compute the posterior probability distribution of each training example's label. By analyzing the concentration of label frequencies, BLRM detects potential mislabels and undergoes a refinement process to correct them, subsequently optimizing the network's performance. We thoroughly test BLRM across a variety of networks, training methods, and noisy data scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness in labeling corrections and network improvements. Moreover, BLRM is compared to existing methods that refine labels, with results highlighting its superiority. Moreover, the mechanism is successfully applied to a real-world issue, the repair of a network trained on the corrupted MNIST dataset to recover from incorrect labels, with BLRM outperforming alternative repair methods. Lastly, the research examines the relationship between the network's performance and labeling refinement thresholds, demonstrating a consistent improvement in robustness with increasing label accuracy, with BLRM having a lesser impact on this improvement. The paper concludes by proposing a novel approach, the Bayesian consensus network, that capitalizes on BLRM's label refinement capabilities to achieve a network configuration that is more sample-efficient, thereby achieving a consistent boost in robustness at all levels of data corruption. The results suggest that optimizing a network's parameters, rather than just its labels, is crucial in unlocking the full potential of deep neural networks. Currently, size-encoding termination proofs are complex and usually made by hand, but researchers have hypothesized that using clock-minimizing methods could simplify these complex proofs. Although previous methods primarily focused on minimalization via substitution, recent advancements in operational semantics have revealed a more flexible and clock-minimizing approach known as generalized operational semantics. This paper demonstrates that this approach is effective not only in minimizing clocks but also termination proofs themselves. Clock-minimization significantly reduces complex termination proofs associated with size-encoding, enabling simpler manual verification processes. Additionally, simplified proofs may reveal new insights or relationships that were previously difficult to detect. For instance, in some cases, termination proofs reveal a surprising pattern where a program terminates under a specific size limit and can consequently accept any input within that size limit, a phenomenon only apparent in simplified proofs. This pattern highlights a novel practical application of simplified size-encoding termination proofs. By simplifying complex termination proofs, we may uncover additional practical applications and insights that were previously detectable only with great effort. Building upon previous clock-minimizing methods, our novel approach extends its applicability to programs that use a greater range of size-based control flow mechanisms, as well as size-based function calls. We have successfully simplified several complex size-encoding termination proofs, revealing new insights and a deeper understanding of various program patterns. For example, in one instance, simplifying the termination proof for the Fibonacci function revealed a clear first-order linear recurrence pattern. We have made this methodology reusable through the creation of a modularized size-based code analyzer tool that can identify clock-minimizing transformations in size-based control flow graphs, generalized operational semantics, and size-based function call graphs. This new tool allows for the automatic extraction of termination proofs and can identify equivalent clock-minimizing transformations for size-based function call graphs that were previously unfeasible to detect manually. By simplifying complex termination proofs, we may uncover additional practical applications and insights that were previously detectable only with great effort and manual analysis. In the context of large eddy simulation (LES) and direct numerical simulation (DNS), this paper introduces a novel approach for modeling the interaction between turbulent flows and solid walls. A wall model, based on the concept of the hairpin packet and in-phase spiral vortices, is developed to describe this interaction. This model is similar to the earlier coherent structure model, but it differs in its interpretation of the wall-attached structures. Additionally, the solution of the momentum wall-layer equations is modified to include the effects of the hairpin packet and in-phase spiral vortices. Specifically, the model uses a minimal consensus model to describe the effects of the wall-attached structures on the wall stress and spanwise pressure gradient. Comparative analyses of the sub-scale stress term and spanwise pressure gradient of the original and modified models show that the modified model performs better. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is evaluated by applying the divergence theorem to incorporate a rough surface effect into the models, which leads to improved results. Comparative simulations of the LES-DNS model with different wall models show that the modified model performs better than the original model. Furthermore, the inclusion of the rough surface effect in the modified model results in even better performance. Overall, the modified model performs similarly to the well-established filtered large Eddy simulation (LES) of wall-bounded flows. This performance comparison reinforces the idea that the hairpin packet and in-phase spiral vortices are the fundamental components of the coherent structural unit (CSU) of the wall-attached structures in turbulence. Based on these findings, a new understanding and interpretation of the CSU of turbulence are proposed. While previous models assumed that the CSU is composed of spiral vortices and hyperbolic points, this research reveals that the hairpin packet is a better representation of the structures. Specifically, the packet's in-phase spiral vortices and hyperbolic points correspond to the vortical and stagnation structures, respectively. This new understanding and the proposed model's performance suggest that the hairpin packet CSU is a more realistic interpretation of the generally accepted concept. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that the incorporation of the hairpin packet CSU into a wall model, when combined with a rough surface effect, can compete favorably with other wall models that are based on the older understanding of the CSU. As such, this research opens the door for the use of the hairpin packet CSU in future research on the simulation and modeling of wall-bounded flows in turbulence. Gravitational potentials in astrophysical research often require solving complex, non-symmetric partial differential equations (PDEs) that are computationally intensive, particularly when dealing with irregular grids. To optimize performance while maintaining accuracy, a hybrid approach combining Fast Multipole Method (FMM) and kernel approximation is employed to solve these equations in a more efficient manner. This method utilizes hierarchical data structures and is based on the standard kernel approximation method but improves solving times by leveraging FMM when conditions are met. The optimization strategy focuses on parameter selection to balance accuracy and computational speed. The hybrid approach is validated against analytical and numerical benchmarks and is shown to improve both memory usage and solving times compared to the traditional kernel approximation method, making it a potential tool for large-scale astrophysical simulations involving time-dependent gravitational potential calculations. Examples of applicable scenarios are given, including the simulation of fluid dynamics with gravitationally interacting objects or the calculation of a planet's potential influenced by other celestial bodies. The proposed algorithm can also be extended to support Taylor series instead of kernel approximations for additional accuracy when necessary. Policy cloning has emerged as a strategy to directly learn a policy from an expert's behavior. Despite its potential, cloning policies efficiently in high-dimensional systems remains a significant challenge. This study reveals that augmented policy cloning can enhance the effectiveness of this approach by leveraging per-action feedback. By incorporating task rewards as action-conditioned objectives, the expert's behavior is modified to include these objectives, enabling the student policy to learn these objectives more easily. Results from trials in a two-finger manipulation task with a 11-dimensional action space demonstrate that augmented cloning significantly improves the ability of a student policy to match an expert's performance. Additionally, both quantitative and qualitative evaluations confirm that augmented cloning yields better-performing policies compared to traditional cloning methods. This research shows that augmented cloning can effectively transfer an expert's skills to a student policy in complex control scenarios. It also presents a novel method for the expert to provide demonstrations that are beneficial for the student policy to learn. Finally, the paper discusses potential applications of cloned policies as a task-oriented supervision tool for reinforcement learning. This research focuses on enhancing stochastic optimization's communication efficiency.
We introduce a unified framework that encompasses existing techniques, like mini-batching, model averaging, and quantization. We also develop novel methods such as spreading out data across more messages, using information loss to determine communication schedules, and a dynamic communication approach that balances efficiency and convergence. We prove that these strategies not only satisfy key convergence requirements but also improve existing bounds by a linear factor. Furthermore, a fundamental framework unifies both conventional and advanced methods, allowing us to derive the optimal number of message rounds under certain conditions. To determine the optimal communication strategy, we suggest a simple, model-free procedure that balances the need for faster convergence and reduced communication overhead. We verify the efficacy of our approach using stochastic convex optimization and multi-task learning applications. Specifically, in a distributed matrix multiplication test, we achieve significant reductions in communication bandwidth by transmitting just one bit per parameter at certain stages. This research lays the groundwork for a fundamental understanding of communication complexity in stochastic optimization and opens up new avenues for optimizing distributed stochastic optimization methods. Furthermore, integrating our techniques with early stopping yields better results than solely relying on termination based on performance metrics. To facilitate future research, we identify areas for potential improvement and propose new strategies to further refine the optimization process. The code developed for this research is openly available at the URL https://github.com/milov/stochastic-communication. Additionally, integrating our techniques with termination based on early stopping yields better outcomes than terminating the process according to sole performance metrics, thus providing a basic framework for optimizing communication efficiency in distributed stochastic optimization without requiring specific convergence guarantees. Furthermore, integrating our techniques with termination based on metrics that combine the performance of the model with its convergence speed offers a middle ground that is missing in current methods. This research lays the groundwork for a fundamental understanding of communication complexity in stochastic optimization and opens up new avenues for further optimization techniques. Lastly, a series of future research directions are proposed including leveraging non-binary encoding, explicitly handling non-concave objectives, and deriving optimal communication strategies for specific problems, thus providing a roadmap for potential advancements in this field. The research presented here contributes knowledge towards efficiently training large-scale, distributed machine learning models by optimizing communication strategies. To facilitate future research, the results obtained highlight several areas where improvement is needed and potential avenues for derived optimal communication strategies are identified, thus providing a roadmap for potential advancements in this field. In particular, proposing quantization as a means to reduce communication bandwidth while maintaining convergence efficiency is a significant contribution of this research, thus enabling the efficient distributed training

While BERT models are renowned for acrobatic tasks in resource-rich settings, they frequently stumble in countries with limited access to technology. Transfer learning between languages with common roots appears to be a viable solution, allowing model training to thrive even in environments with scarce data. We carry out a thorough comparison of various transfer learning techniques using contextualized models, encompassing BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA, and XLNet. Our experiment showcases the effectiveness of transfer learning in enhancing predictions on low-resource languages, revealing substantial cross-lingual interdependencies in the process. Notably, ELECTRA's superior performance across a range of resource levels makes it an ideal choice for applications involving transfer learning. Our code and data are publicly available for review.

Expert drivers have decades of experience informing their judgments on driver and road characteristics, however their individual insights are dispersed and difficult to build upon collectively. In our research, we interviewed five experienced drivers and used their input to create a series of driving scenario questions which we then distributed to a larger group of drivers, along with a set of conditions relating to road and weather. By gathering additional driving data and relating it to the original scenario questions, we generated numerical outcomes representing various driving behaviors under different environmental conditions. By analyzing the responses, we identified both consistent and divergent driving behaviors, with a notable distinction in responses to rainy versus dry conditions. Our analysis further indicates that driver reviews are more closely tied to the prevailing weather rather than driver personality. Ultimately, our method presents a promising avenue for utilizing expert insights to inform the assessment of driver behaviors, thereby facilitating the development of more accurate models of driving simulation. To investigate the connection that exists between fluid dynamics in narrow channels and magnetic levitation, we examine the hydrodynamic balance achieved by reducing gravitational influence on heavy, dense fluids within a specific setup.  Initial disturbances for this study were generated by placing a lightweight, magnetic piece near the surface of a dense fluid flowing in a horizontal direction, which caused it to rise due to magnetohydrodynamic repulsion.  This process is then analyzed using high-speed videography.  Two distinct methods are presented for calculating the force exerted on the dense fluid by a magnetic field, both of which incorporate corrections to minimize light-induced disturbances.  One of these methods measures the force directly through the density and magnetic field, while the other method views the force as inducing rotational movement in the dense fluid.  These calculations yield consistent results that are comparable to theoretical predictions obtained using simplified models.  Ultimately, we demonstrate that magnetic levitation provides a dense, stable, and extendable platform for exploring hydrodynamic balance and the behavior of dense fluids under magnetic fields.  This platform also enables the study of specific gravitational influences, such as those that exist in vertical channels.  Lastly, we identify a threshold magnitude of magnetic field magnitude below which light-induced disturbances become significant, which necessitate larger cross-sectional areas in order to minimize these disturbances. The development of this setup, which combines magnetic levitation with hydrodynamic balance, offers a wealth of opportunities for exploring photo-induced disturbances, which can be eliminated, and the connection between magnetic fields and dense fluid dynamics under gravitational influence.  This platform also provides a means for accurately calculating magnetic field intensities, which can be utilized in various areas of research focused on dense fluid dynamics.  Finally, we identify inherent limitations that must be addressed in order to achieve a comprehensive understanding of magnetic fields and dense fluid dynamics.  These limitations, which can be overcome through advancements in experimental techniques, enable the establishment of a unique technological advancement, which leverages magnetic levitation, light-induced disturbances, and dense fluid dynamics to create stable, 3D crystal structures from superfluids within specific magnetic fields.  This breakthrough reveals new connections between magnetic fields, dense fluid dynamics, and light-induced disturbances, which can be utilized in multiple areas of research focused on condensed matter physics. This pioneering framework is currently being applied to guide decisions regarding the management of underground telecommunications infrastructure in Montreal.
