This new framework has significant implications for machine learning approaches, particularly in unsupervised contexts, by allowing us to develop theories and methods that can be broadly applied across different domains. Moreover, we provide concrete examples of how this idea can be implemented in ranking systems, uncovering novel properties and characteristics of the resulting system. Ultimately, our aim is to explore the practical advantages of this novel system in real-world scenarios. Key aspects of our approach include its ability to handle false positives in any type of ranking system, operate without supervision, guarantee stability, and ensure that the new rankings we generate are preferential to the original ones. By building on existing ranking systems, our novel transformation allows us to achieve these objectives in a coherent and meaningful manner. Specifically, we have devised a new box re-ranking objective formula – known as the sum of the top weights – that effectively addresses the challenge of false positives. Subsequently, we have developed algorithms that achieve the optimal result for this new objective, building on the concept of the top-k AUC. In the experiments we conducted, our results demonstrated the effectiveness of this new approach, which outperformed the traditional top-k re-ranking objective in the context of false positive suppression, even when the two methods were applied in different ways (proactive vs. reactive). By further investigating the properties of the top-k AUC, we have uncovered its relationship to other important concepts in machine learning, such as calibration and the Expected Calibration Graph. In the final part of our research, we have established the measures of the width and depth of the top items in a ranking system, which provide valuable insights into the characteristics of these systems. These width and depth metrics also enable us to differentiate between various ranking system designs. Moreover, we have established a bound on how much the expected AUC value changes when the size of the ranking list is modified. By revealing the inherent non-decomposability of the top-k AUC, we have also established a bound on how much the inversion of the top-k AUC value is affected by changes in individual item preferences. Subsequently, we have explored the practical implications of these properties and have developed efficient methods to manipulate various aspects of ranking systems, which we verified in the course of our experiments. The incorporation of domain-specific features in neural machine translation has been shown to improve translation quality, however it also affects output fluency and coherence. To minimize these negative impacts, we investigate a novel approach that uses a syntax-aware attention model. This model identifies relevant sentence segments in the source language, prioritizing those with analogous syntactic structures to the target sentence and thus reducing incorrect translations. By using this style-gate model, the system can easily exclude irrelevant information from being translated, as a result the translation quality, fluency and sentence order are all preserved. Experiments conducted on English-Japanese language pairs produce significant improvements in translation quality, specifically a 1.38 and 0.27 increase in BLEU scores in the ATOMIC and WALS domains respectively. Additionally there is a notable reduction in grammatical errors, specifically 0.63 and 0.20 decrease in JGR in the ATOMIC and WALS domains respectively. To further verify the effectiveness of the style-gate model, a complementary analysis is performed in the opposite direction, specifically extracting Japanese sentences and translating them into English while suppressing similar stylistic elements. Results from this reverse experiment confirm the style-gate model's capability of preserving output fluency and coherence. Predicting the distribution and depth of these snow lines is vital for understanding planet formation, particularly for gas giants and super-Earths. Due to the difficulties in precisely modeling protoplanetary discs, particularly for objects beyond the tidal disruption boundary of the host star, we adopt a statistical physics-based approach called the "disc ensemble method" developed recently to analyze global trends. The experiment is repeated multiple times, and both the classical processing of data and quantum noise reduction are performed to enhance the precision of the estimate. The divisibility of the resulting state ensemble is guaranteed, and a formula is derived for calculating the expected value of any measurable, as well as its statistical uncertainty. The protocol's performance is evaluated by considering two key metrics: the first is the precision of the estimate, defined as the expected value of the square of the estimate's standard deviation; while the second is the statistical uncertainty, defined as the standard deviation of the estimate's distribution. In a multi-task linear regression scenario with any number of tasks, where we have an unlimited amount of labeled data available, the objective (to minimize prediction error while avoiding overfitting to a single task) is easily achieved through an approach that adapts to all tasks without any modifications. However, the situation becomes complicated in an algorithmic sense when we're restricted to a limited number of labeled samples per task. Our research examines the implications of these two distinct settings - one where sample efficiency is the primary concern and another with an emphasis on adaptability - and studies a specific type of algorithm known as square root estimators, which is known to perform well in a single-task setting. Our findings reveal that square root estimators are suboptimal in a multi-task setting where sample efficiency is in question. Conversely, we present a new square root estimators algorithm that efficiently uses samples across all tasks, thus minimizing the sample complexity of square root estimators in a multi-task setting. Our analysis also highlights the optimality of our algorithm by showing it reaches the minimum possible sample size. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that any square root estimators algorithm that efficiently uses samples across all tasks will necessarily converge towards optimal performance as tasks increase, thus achieving optimal adaptability. Our findings also reveal that achieving both optimal sample efficiency and adaptability may be impossible for certain types of algorithms, and that achieving adaptability is inherently difficult when the number of tasks increases, unless task-specific patterns have a significant overlap. Our research presents a new framework for categorizing algorithms based on the number of tasks. Our research findings also highlight the intriguing fact that achieving optimal sample efficiency and adaptability may be impossible for certain types of algorithms, and that achieving adaptability is inherently difficult when the number of tasks increases, unless task-specific patterns have a significant overlap. Our research findings also highlight a trade-off between adaptability and sample efficiency in square root estimators, and presents a new algorithm that achieves optimal sample efficiency across all tasks without any modifications, and demonstrates that any algorithm that achieves optimal sample efficiency also adapts to varying task numbers. Our research presents a new algorithm known as square root estimators, which is known to perform well in a multi-task setting. Our research findings also highlight a connection between the sample efficiency of square root estimators and adaptability. Our research finds that when the number of tasks increases, square root estimators tend to overfit and lose their sample efficiency. Our research presents a new algorithm known as square root estimators, which is known to perform well in a multi-task setting.

Baber and Talbot have proved a central result that demonstrates the existence of a minimum tau density for r-uniform graphs. Specifically, they have shown that for any value of r greater than or equal to three, there is a minimum tau density existing for r-uniform graphs, which can be expressed as a function of the rth power of the square root of two. Furthermore, they have determined that this minimum tau density is approximately 0.5 when r is equal to three, while it is approximately 0.81 for r equal to four. Our research builds upon these findings by investigating and providing exact values of minimum tau density for various r-uniform graphs when they contain complete r-partite structures. We have also identified a minimum tau density of 1/2 for the (4K,2K) 16-partite configuration and established an upper and lower bound of 1/2 for general r-uniform p-tuple free graphs when p is less than or equal to (r-1)/2, which closely approaches the known result of tau being equal to the rth power of the square root of two for r-uniform graphs. Furthermore, we have confirmed that a particular r-uniform graph containing 52 triples or more is 3-uniform, which closely approaches the known result of tau being equal to 52/125 for 3-uniform graphs. Our research method involves applying the Erdos-Sos conjecture to the Ramseyan r-uniform p-tuple free graph problem. We have also validated the Baber-Talbot theorem by establishing that if tau is greater than the tau lower bound of the r-uniform graph H, then H contains an r-uniform r-partite structure consisting of the complete graph K_r(p_i) for all i equal to one to k where the sum of p_i is equal to p. We have also given an approximation of the minimum tau density for r-uniform graphs, which closely approaches the rth power of the square root of two. Our research contributes an easier proof of the r-uniform graph tau result by showing that for r greater than or equal to three, there is an r-uniform graph with exactly r triples whose tau is equal to the rth power of the square root of two. The concept of contrastive causation is crucial in legal definitions of harm, implying that a harm exists if it can be distinguished as causing an undesirable outcome as opposed to a desirable one. However, when applied to complex cases with multiple causal factors, this definition runs into difficulties. This challenge can be addressed through the use of probabilistic inquiry and formal models that help evaluate the presence of contrastive causation by assessing the likelihood of an undesirable versus a desirable outcome given a particular set of conditions. By doing so, we can refine the definition of harm through the application of principles such as de minimis and to render decisions in intricate cases involving pre-existing conditions and their interplay with new harms. Ultimately, this approach can be used to develop decision theories by establishing criteria for choosing between competing hypotheses about causes and effects. This model builds upon the hyperbolic heat conduction equation, incorporating memory effects and non-linear interactions between heat flux and temperature gradients. Drawing from non-linear non-equilibrium thermodynamics, a combined heat flux and heat gradient dependence is introduced. The model also accounts for the relaxation phenomena of non-equilibrium processes through a distinct time characteristic associated with the deviation of non-equilibrium temperatures from the classical Boltzmann temperature. An analytical solution to the non-linear two-temperature model is presented for a specific heat absorption process. This solution verifies the physical plausibility of the model and its mathematical coherence through various asymptotic analyses. Our results show that incorporating peak forecasts into basic forecasting methods yields significant improvements in demand forecasting accuracy, particularly during peak hours. The goal of empirical machine learning is to create accurate predictions from given data, with principles based on statistical sampling. A related area, deductive machine learning, aims to incorporate prior knowledge into the modeling process, enhancing the capabilities of machine learning algorithms. This research examines the intersection of empirical and deductive methods by analyzing the effects of known parameters on predictive models. By characterizing data distributions as dependent on known parameters, we develop a theoretical framework for combining data-driven and structural knowledge within predictive models. This investigation reveals opportunities for improving prediction accuracy by considering the impacts of structural assumptions. An adaptive approach is also proposed for determining optimal structural parameters, allowing for tailored predictions tailored to specific scenarios. This methodology is successfully applied to the field of renewable energy, where a sophisticated model incorporating various knowledge components achieves superior prediction performance compared to standard statistical models. Experimental results confirm that incorporating structural knowledge can enhance prediction accuracy, and that the proposed adaptive method consistently yields optimal outcomes. Additionally, this research introduces several theoretical concepts, including the notions of structural assumptions, operational scenarios, and structural parameters. The developed methodology also lays the groundwork for applying semantic techniques, like knowledge bases and ontologies, to further advance machine learning algorithms. By systematically analyzing the effects of known parameters on predictive models, we gain insights into the roles of empirical data and structural knowledge in shaping predictive models. And by distinguishing between scenario-specific and general structural parameters, we identify predictive models that are invariant under certain transformations, revealing opportunities for developing machine learning algorithms that leverage these symmetries. The proposed methodology also addresses the challenge of sparsity in predictive models, showing that incorporating structural knowledge can lead to simplified models, and that the amount of sparsity generated by structural knowledge is a non-decreasing function of the model's complexity. Overall, this research contributes to the understanding of the interplay between empirical data-driven and structural knowledge-driven machine learning methods, and identifies predictive models that are invariant under these symmetries as a promising area of semantic analysis. As a final point, our results reveal the potential of tailor-made machine learning algorithms that account for specific scenario variability, and reiterate the importance of incorporating structural knowledge to improve prediction accuracy. And as a direct application of these findings, our models outperform standard statistical models on multiple prediction tasks, underlining the need for more sophisticated algorithms that capture complex correlations, including those based on knowledge components. Our research reveals that vacuum fluctuations of light cause certain polariton states to collapse with a different timescale in systems consisting of a quantum dot embedded in a cavity filled with an anisotropic dielectric material. Through theoretical analysis based on a multilevel model, we explain how variations in the dielectric material's orientation impact the polariton states and predict a measurable shift in the collisionless damping phenomenon. This effect can be experimentally observed by tracking the deformation of polariton branches under increased excitation intensity. Furthermore, our findings can be applied to investigate the role of vacuum fluctuations in a broader range of cavity-based systems. As a consequence of these findings, researchers may be able to utilize intense light to compensate for the destabilizing influence of vacuum fluctuations, thus opening up possibilities for controlling polariton states and polariton-induced phenomena. This breakthrough could be further developed into a new platform for quantum information processing and could also facilitate the creation of novel applications based on polaritonic states. The observed properties are consistent across a wide temperature range, encompassing both near-field and far-field regimes, and remain sensitive to microwave radiation. Additionally, our detailed calculations accurately recreate the latest experimental findings as reported in J. Phys.: Photonics, 4, 025802 (2022). The predicted behavior is largely controlled by the polariton's collisionless damping rate, allowing for a direct comparison between theoretical and experimental results. The development of this technique may also lead to the detection of vacuum fluctuations produced by gravitational waves, as reported in the LIGO/Virgo collaboration's most recent observations. Since the observed phenomena occur at high temperatures and have coherently controlled origins, researchers may be able to utilize these effects to create a collisionless damping interface, paving the way for the development of novel techniques and applications. The predicted behavior remains stable across a wide temperature range, encompassing both low and high temperatures, and could also be further developed to detect and manipulate photonic and excitonic states. Furthermore, our research reveals that the collisionless damping phenomenon is largely influenced by the presence of a transverse electromagnetic field, as generated by the dielectric material's anisotropy, rather than by the typically considered longitudinal field components. The predicted effect can be further optimized by adjusting the dielectric material's anisotropy, thus allowing for a direct fine-tuning of the collisionless damping rate. This breakthrough could also be further developed to achieve the quantum coherences modulation, which has recently been reported in the cavity quantum electrodynamics setup with a quantum dot. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices can't yet maintain stability across multiple operations, so we suggest utilizing their limitations to our advantage. By harnessing their noise for a specific purpose, we've developed a method to determine if a given quantum state is fully separable without needing to achieve quantum supremacy. This method converts the separability problem into a series of local measurements that can be performed on NISQ devices, utilizing their inherent noise to produce a negative output and thus confirm non-separability or refine the range of possible pure states. This technique is efficient, requiring only basic quantum circuit operations and a limited number of repetitions, making it suitable for states composed of 10-15 qubits or smaller. By applying this protocol to a specific Bell-diagonal state, we've precisely calculated the probability of obtaining a negative outcome, confirming that it corresponds to a fully separable mixed state. This technique is not only useful for characterizing quantum systems, but also offers insights into potential applications for NISQ devices. Additionally, we've explored the theoretical performance of this protocol using ideal machines that can generate Bell-diagonal states, resulting in a novel method for estimating the cross-correlations of quantum states based on the probability distribution of white noise. Our work thus showcases the practical value of NISQ devices in quantum information processing, even in the absence of quantum supremacy, by harnessing their noise to solve complex problems and harness their inherent limitations as a resource. This research demonstrates that noisy NISQ devices can facilitate a precise characterization of informationally complete states, marking an important breakthrough in understanding their capabilities and revealing the counterintuitive property of noise as a tool for state analysis. The protocol we've developed is now listed as Algorithm 1, along with its implementation on current quantum hardware as quantum-coarse-graining, potentially opening doors to new applications in the NISQ era. This technique has been confirmed to work not only for Bell-diagonal states but also for arbitrary multi-qubit states, utilizing noise-induced collapses on any quantum system without specific assumptions. We've further shown that noise-induced analysis can be an efficient method for estimating quantum correlations in systems that can already stabilize coherences, such as systems utilizing double-quantum coherences and being monitored by environment-induced collapses, providing an alternative to noise-induced collapses. We develop a gradient flow framework for addressing ill-posed problems, which we term backflow problems, as any solution would imply a backwards flow where a ball is shrunk into a point. The standard stop-time in algorithms has been the first time the energy's minimiser is reached, but this approach leads to inaccurate results with significant overestimation, as demonstrated with a simple example. A more suitable stop-time is when the energy's gradient becomes zero, but this is challenging to use in algorithms. We overcame this by employing a stop-time based on the average behavior of the energy's gradient over the current time-step and the previous one, which results in a more precise solution. A numerical demonstration of this new stop-time is presented using the problem of shrinking a ball. As a result, a more precise solution can be obtained by combining this approach with a non-metric discrete-time gradient flow. We compared the performance of our new stop-time with the standard approach in experiments involving the problem of shrinking a ball. The findings show that, whereas the standard stop-time leads to unrealistic downwards scaling of the ball, which becomes increasingly underestimed as the scale factor decreases, our new stop-time produces more accurate results, as well as accurately captures the dynamics of the problem and its solution. These experimental results confirm that, by choosing the correct stop-time, a precise approximation of the solution to a backflow problem can be obtained. We extend our new stop-time approach to a complex problem, the problem of shrinking a ball with an irregular surface, which poses significant computational challenges due to its highly varying curvature. These challenges are overcome by combining our discrete-time gradient flow with a discrete projection, which yields a precise solution to the problem. A plot showing the actual shrinking of the ball and the corresponding stop-time-based solution demonstrates the accuracy of our new approach. Experimental results indicate a strong correlation between the stop-time-based solution and the problem's actual solution, which suggests that our discrete projection-based approach is effective. Furthermore, a comparison between the stop-time-based solution and the problem's actual solution as well as a discrete projection-based approach to an average action-based solution confirms their strong correlation. The research demonstrates the applicability of discrete gradient flow with non-metric backflow problems and non-metric discrete projection-based approach to an average action-based solution for a broader category of problems, which are termed semiwell-posed problems, which are problems which are not ill-posed but also not quite well-posed either, which means they are not approximated by gradient flow. Differing from traditional methods using pixel values or gradients, this constructor is impervious to occlusions. It calculates the depth by averaging the logarithms of intensity ratios in local clusters, which is then translated into a normalized cross-correlation score to trigger odometry signals. The constructor has been successfully validated with simulated data and real-world experiments on a robotic wheeled platform. In the simulated test, it was observed that using logarithmic intensity ratios led to a more accurate representation of the scene layout, resulting in a more detailed point cloud. In the real-world test, it was found that using the proposed constructor in semi-dense SLAM enabled the creation of high-quality 3D maps and reconstructed the robot's interactions with its environment successfully, with the added bonus of operating without sensitivity to occlusions. However, it's worth noting that the constructor has a moderate requirement for texture in the scene. Moreover, it was observed that the constructor's performance declines in areas of varying illumination. A possible direction for further research could be the development of a strategy to utilize multi-spectral or active sensing techniques, which can operate effectively in varying illumination conditions. Home WiFi networks frequently set device association using default methods such as channel load and signal strength. While channel load association reduces congestion, signal strength association maintains network balance. This paper introduces an innovative association method that optimizes device placement for minimal network congestion. The new method calculates an optimization factor for each device and associates it with the access point that minimizes congestion, has sufficient signal strength, and meets specific service requirements. The proposed technique encourages devices to associate with access points that have less crowded channels, thus slowly moving devices away from congested channels. The results show this method reduces congestion in channel load association and improves throughput and delay in signal strength association. The method, however, requires optimization to balance these benefits with signal strength. The channel load aware association method was further improved to promote in-home device association, thus reducing congestion caused by external devices. The improved method encourages in-home devices to associate with access points that minimize congestion, thus promoting device balance in the network. The results show this method promotes in-home device association, thus reducing congestion and improving overall device association in the network.
